column1: What is DM? + Explain steps of KDD process
column4:
DM
  • Extraction of interesting patterns/knowledge from large data.
  • Interesting \(=\) non-trivial \(+\) implicit \(+\) previously unknown \(+\) potentially useful.
  • Not retrieval:
    • Query tool \(\rightarrow\) answers what you already know to ask.
    • DM \(\rightarrow\) finds patterns you didnt know to look for.
  • Also called: KDD, knowledge extraction, data/pattern analysis, data archaeology, data dredging, BI.
Not DM
  • Phone-book lookup, SELECT AVG(salary), web search \(\rightarrow\) info retrieval (query states exactly what is wanted).
Descriptive DM
  • Characterise the general properties of data.
  • Unsupervised.
  • “What is in data? Unusual patterns?”
  • Clustering, association, summarisation, visualisation.
Predictive DM
  • Infer unknown \(Y=f(X)\) from known \(X\).
  • Supervised.
  • “Which customers leave in 6 months?”
  • Classification, regression, prediction.
DM vs KDD
  • Strictly: DM \(=\) one step of KDD (the step that runs the algorithms).
  • In practice treated as synonyms. IOE papers use them interchangeably.
  • If Q says “steps of data mining” \(\rightarrow\) write KDD steps.
KDD: 7 steps (Han & Kamber) \(\rightarrow\) default answer
  1. Data cleaning: rm noise, smooth outliers, fill missing, fix inconsistency.
  2. Data integration: combine multiple heterogeneous sources.
  3. Data selection: retrieve only task-relevant data.
  4. Data transformation: normalise, aggregate, generalise, discretise.
  5. Data mining: apply algorithms. Essential step.
  6. Pattern evaluation: keep truly interesting patterns (support, confidence, lift, novelty).
  7. Knowledge presentation: visualise + represent for user.
Steps 1–4 \(=\) data preparation \(\approx\) 60% of effort.

column1: Origin of DM: why it emerged
column4:
Confluence of disciplines
  • DB systems
  • Statistics
  • Machine learning
  • AI / pattern recognition
  • Visualisation
  • High-performance computing
Drivers
  • Automated collection \(\rightarrow\) data explosion (POS scanners, txn logs, sensors, satellites, Web).
  • Cheap storage \(\rightarrow\) hoarding became rational. Analysis did not keep pace.
  • Competition \(\rightarrow\) unmined data \(=\) wasted asset.
Why traditional/manual analysis fails
  • Enormity (TB scale).
  • High dimensionality (1000s of attrs).
  • Sources heterogeneous \(+\) distributed.
  • Data collected for ops, not analysis \(\rightarrow\) noisy, incomplete, inconsistent.
DM vs query tools (SQL)
  • SQL: must know exactly what you want. DM: only vaguely.
  • SQL \(\rightarrow\) facts/aggregates. DM \(\rightarrow\) patterns/trends.
  • SQL: deterministic retrieval. DM: ML/statistical search.
  • Hidden relations:
    • SQL cant trace them
    • DM finds them automatically

column1: “The world is data rich but information poor”. Justify.
column4:
1. State paradox: TBs stored, decisions still on intuition. Data \(\ne\) info \(\ne\) knowledge.
  2. Data rich: POS logs, bank txns, telecom call records, remote sensing, Web. Growth automated.
  3. Info poor, why:
    • Volume defeats manual inspection.
    • Data is operational \(\rightarrow\) noisy, incomplete, inconsistent.
    • Scattered across heterogeneous systems.
    • Query tools answer only what is asked.
    • Shortage of analysts.
  4. Consequence: “data tombs” \(=\) archives written, never read. Decisions made w/o evidence already paid for.
  5. Resolution:
    • DW consolidates \(+\) cleans
    • DM extracts the patterns
    • Data \(\rightarrow\) Info \(\rightarrow\) Knowledge \(\rightarrow\) Decision
  6. Eg: retail chain holds millions of receipts (rich) but cant say which products sell together (poor) until association analysis gives {nappies} \(\Rightarrow\) {beer}.

column1: “Data mining turns a large collection of data into knowledge”. Justify
column4:
The ladder, one rung at a time
  1. Data: raw recorded facts, no context. Eg 2 million supermarket receipt lines.
  2. Information: data aggregated and given context by querying. Eg “nappies sold 4,200 units last month”. A DW and OLAP get you here, and this is as far as a query tool can go — it answers only what you thought to ask.
  3. Knowledge: patterns that hold across the data and were not asked for. Eg “customers buying nappies on Friday evening also buy beer”. Only data mining produces this rung, because only it searches the space of possible patterns.
  4. Decision / wisdom: acting on the pattern. Eg move the beer display beside the nappies, and measure the lift in basket value.
Why the step to knowledge is data mining's alone
  • Queries are deductive, mining is inductive. SQL retrieves what you specify; mining induces a general rule from the instances.
  • It is automatic and exhaustive: Apriori tests every itemset the thresholds allow, far more hypotheses than an analyst would think to write.
  • The output is predictive, not just descriptive: a classifier built on past data labels tuples that do not exist yet.
  • The patterns are required to be valid, novel, useful and understandable — Fayyad's four conditions. “Novel” is what makes it knowledge: a pattern you already knew is information, not knowledge.
Close with the qualifier
  • DM does not turn all data into knowledge. Garbage in, garbage out: without preprocessing (Ch 2) it turns noise into confident nonsense, and without pattern evaluation (§4.1) it reports rules that are strong but false.

column1: Architecture of a typical DM system (+Fig)
column4:
• Data sources: DB, DW, WWW, other repos.
  • DB/DW server: fetches data relevant to the request.
  • Knowledge base: domain knowledge guiding search \(+\) judging interestingness (concept hierarchies, user beliefs, constraints).
  • DM engine: characterisation, association, classification, clustering, outlier, evolution analysis.
  • Pattern evaluation: applies interestingness measures. Best pushed into the engine so dull patterns are never generated.
  • UI: specify task, browse schemas/hierarchies, visualise results.

column1: What is a DW? Write its key features.
column4:
Definition (Inmon)
  • DW \(=\) subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, non-volatile collection of data supporting management decision-making.
  • Memorise as S-I-T-N \(\rightarrow\) this is the whole “key features” answer.
  • S = Subject-oriented
    • Organised around subjects (customer, product, sales), not daily ops.
    • Data useless for decisions is excluded.
  • I = Integrated
    • Built from heterogeneous sources (relational DBs, flat files, txn records).
    • Cleaning \(+\) integration force consistent naming, encoding, units.
    • \(\rightarrow\) 1 name per entity.
  • T = Time-variant
    • Long history (5–10 yrs).
    • Every key structure carries a time element.
    • Operational DB holds only the current value.
  • N = Non-volatile
    • Physically separate. No operational update.
    • Only 2 ops: initial load \(+\) access.
    • \(\rightarrow\) no txn processing, recovery or concurrency control needed.
  • Data warehousing \(=\) the process of building \(+\) using a DW (extract, transform operational data, load into central store).

column1: How is DW diff from a DB? How are they similar?
column4:
Operational DB (OLTP)Data warehouse (OLAP)
PurposeRun day-to-day businessSupport analysis \(+\) decisions
ContentCurrent, detailedHistorical, summarised \(+\) detailed
DesignHighly normalised, many tables (ER)De-normalised, few tables; star/snowflake
AccessShort read/write txnsLong, complex, read-mostly
UsersClerks, DBAs, front-lineManagers, analysts, execs
Unit of workSimple txnComplex query
Records/queryTensMillions
Size100 MB–GB100 GB–TB
Similarities verified/added
  • Both persistent, managed data stores.
  • Both usually on a relational DBMS.
  • Both use schemas, indexes, SQL.
  • Both enforce integrity \(+\) security.
  • DW is built from the DBs.
Why keep them separate
  • Performance: opposite tuning.
    • DBMS \(\rightarrow\) OLTP (indexing, concurrency, recovery)
    • DW \(\rightarrow\) OLAP (multidim views, consolidation)
    • both on 1 system degrades both
  • Missing data: decisions need history ops DBs dont keep.
  • Consolidation: needs aggregation across heterogeneous sources.
  • Data quality: inconsistent codes/formats reconciled once, centrally.

column1: Explain DW architecture with its analytical processing
column4:
(a) Three-tier architecture (Han & Kamber) \(\rightarrow\) standard answer
  • Bottom tier \(=\) warehouse DB server (relational).
    • Data pulled via gateways: ODBC, OLE-DB, JDBC.
    • Back-end tools: extract, clean, transform, load, refresh.
    • Holds metadata repo.
  • Middle tier \(=\) OLAP server (presents data as a cube).
    • ROLAP:
      • extended relational DBMS
      • maps multidim ops \(\rightarrow\) relational ops
      • scales to large data
    • MOLAP:
      • special-purpose server, direct multidim arrays
      • fast, but sparse data wastes space
    • HOLAP:
      • hybrid of the two
      • detail in relational, aggregates in arrays
  • Top tier \(=\) front-end client: query & reporting, analysis, DM tools.
(b) Process / component architecture (form drawn in class notes)
  • Load manager: all extract \(+\) load ops. Fast-loads into temp store, simple transforms.
  • Warehouse manager:
    • consistency \(+\) referential checks
    • merges temp store into the published DW
    • creates indexes \(+\) business views
    • updates aggregations
    • backup \(+\) archive
  • Query manager:
    • directs queries to the right tables
    • stops 1 query starving the system
    • captures query profiles
  • Detailed info: lowest-granularity data retained.
  • Summary info:
    • pre-computed aggregations built by the warehouse manager
    • transient, changes as query profiles change
  • Metadata: data about data. Describes how info is structured, maps sources to a common view.
(c) “…with its analytical processing” \(\rightarrow\) 3 kinds of DW application
  1. Information processing: querying, basic stats, reporting (crosstabs, tables, charts). No new knowledge.
  2. Analytical processing (OLAP): multidim analysis. Roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice, pivot. Summarises, doesnt learn.
  3. Data mining: knowledge discovery from hidden patterns. Creates new knowledge.

column1: What is DW and data mart? (short notes)
column4:
Data mart
  • Subset of a DW, confined to 1 user group / functional area, in its own DB.
  • Dependent: sourced from an enterprise DW \(\rightarrow\) consistent by construction.
  • Independent: populated directly from sources, no central DW \(\rightarrow\) faster to build, risks inconsistency between marts.
  • Benefit:
    • less volume to scan \(\rightarrow\) faster queries
    • each department owns its own structures
  • Eg: departmental store sales mart, bank loan mart.
3 DW models
  • Enterprise warehouse: all subjects, whole org. Cross-functional, large, slow to build.
  • Data mart: subset for a specific group.
  • Virtual warehouse:
    • set of views over operational DBs
    • only some summary views materialised
    • easy to build, but loads the operational systems

column4:
• Star: 1 central fact table (measures \(+\) FKs) \(+\) de-normalised dimension tables. Simple, fast joins.
  • Snowflake: star refined, some dimension hierarchies normalised into smaller sub-dimension tables. Saves space, less redundancy, but more joins \(\rightarrow\) slower.
  • Fact constellation (galaxy): multiple fact tables sharing dimension tables \(=\) collection of stars.
Eg: sales DW
  • Fact Sales: time_key, item_key, branch_key, location_key, units_sold, dollars_sold, avg_sales.
  • location normalised: location \(\rightarrow\) city \(\rightarrow\) province.
  • item \(\rightarrow\) supplier.
  • That normalisation of the dimension hierarchy is what makes it snowflake, not star.
\(\rightarrow\) Full multidim model (cuboids, base/apex, star-schema drawing numerical) sits in Ch 2, OLAP & Multidimensional Data Analysis, where it is examined harder.

column1: How can a DM system be integrated with a DB/DW system?
column4:
1. No coupling
  • Uses no DB/DW function at all.
  • Reads flat file \(\rightarrow\) mines \(\rightarrow\) writes to another file.
  • Simple, but: poor data selection, no scalability, no consistency.
2. Loose coupling
  • Mining system \(\rightarrow\) fetches data from repo managed by DB/DW.
  • Stores results back into a file / designated place in DB.
  • Uses DBMS for storage \(+\) retrieval only.
  • Cant exploit indexing or query optimisation \(\rightarrow\) memory-bound, doesnt scale well.
3. Semi-tight coupling
  • Besides linking, DB/DW provides efficient mining primitives.
  • Primitives: sorting, indexing, aggregation, histogram analysis, multi-way join.
  • \(+\) pre-computed stats: sum, count, max, min.
  • \(\rightarrow\) materially better performance.
4. Tight coupling
  • DM system smoothly integrated into DB/DW as 1 functional component.
  • Mining queries optimised alongside DB queries.
  • Intermediate results can be stored.
  • Scales. Most desirable design.

column1: What is DM? Explain diff data types of attributes in a dataset.
column4:
Attribute
  • Property / characteristic of an object. Eg eye colour, temperature.
  • Also called: variable, field, feature, characteristic.
  • Object \(=\) record, point, case, sample, entity, instance.
  • Same attr \(\rightarrow\) diff value sets (height in ft or m).
  • Diff attrs \(\rightarrow\) same value set, diff properties (ID and age are both int, but ID has no max).
Han & Kamber 3rd ed: 4 types (use this, it is the syllabus ref book)
  • Nominal: names / categories only, no order. Zip code, employee ID, eye colour.
  • Binary: nominal w/ exactly 2 states (0/1).
    • Symmetric: both states equally valuable. Gender.
    • Asymmetric: one state rarer + more important. Disease test P/N. Convention: rarest outcome \(=1\).
  • Ordinal: order meaningful, gap between successive values unknown. {small, medium, large}, grades, mineral hardness.
  • Numeric: measurable quantity.
    • Interval-scaled: gaps meaningful, no true zero. Dates, temp in \(^\circ\)C/\(^\circ\)F.
    • Ratio-scaled: gaps and ratios meaningful, true zero. Temp in K, money, counts, age.
Older N-O-I-R split (Tan; DBK's slide)
  • Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio. Binary folded into nominal.
  • Same content, different grouping. Either scores; H&K's is safer as it names binary explicitly, which the similarity questions depend on.
2nd cut: discrete vs continuous
  • Discrete: finite / countably infinite set. Zip codes, counts, words in a doc. Usually int.
    • Binary \(=\) special case of discrete.
    • Symmetric binary: both states equally valuable (gender).
    • Asymmetric binary: one state rarer + more important (disease test P/N). Matters: Jaccard ignores 0-0 matches, SMC does not.
  • Continuous: real values. Temp, height, weight. Stored as float.
Types of datasets
  • Record
    • Data matrix: \(m\) objects \(\times\) \(n\) numeric attrs \(\rightarrow\) points in \(n\)-dim space.
    • Document data: each doc \(=\) term vector, value \(=\) term frequency.
    • Transaction data: each record \(=\) set of items. Eg grocery basket.
  • Graph: nodes \(+\) links. Eg WWW, molecular structures.
  • Ordered: spatial (geo coords), temporal (\(d=f(t)\)), sequential, sequence data.
Characteristics of structured data
  • Dimensionality \(\rightarrow\) curse of dimensionality (see 2.2).
  • Sparsity: % of cells not populated. Sparsity \(+\) density \(=\) 100.
  • Resolution: patterns depend on the scale you look at.

column1: What is Data Pre-Processing? Explain the major tasks performed in it.
column4:
Why preprocess
  • Real data is dirty: incomplete, noisy, inconsistent.
  • Cause: huge size \(+\) multiple heterogeneous sources.
  • Garbage in \(\rightarrow\) garbage out. Low quality data \(\rightarrow\) low quality mining.
  • Data prep \(\approx\) 60% of total effort in KDD.
5 major tasks (this is the answer)
  1. Data cleaning: fill missing, smooth noise, fix inconsistency, rm duplicates.
  2. Data integration: merge multiple sources into 1 coherent store.
  3. Data transformation: normalise, aggregate, generalise, construct attrs.
  4. Data reduction: smaller volume, same analytical result.
  5. Data discretisation: continuous \(\rightarrow\) intervals (part of reduction).
Answer skeleton 7
  1. Definition \(+\) “why”: dirty data, garbage in garbage out.
  2. Name the 5 tasks.
  3. 2 lines each, with 1 concrete technique per task.
  4. Close: cleaning \(+\) integration dominate the effort.
(a) Data cleaning
Missing values: why
  • Equipment malfunction, misunderstanding at entry, deleted as inconsistent, not considered important, no change recorded.
Noisy data
  • Noise \(=\) random error / variance in a measured variable.
  • Cause: faulty instruments, entry error, transmission error, tech limits, naming inconsistency.
How to handle noise
  • Binning: sort, partition into bins, smooth by bin mean / median / boundary.
  • Regression: fit data to a function.
  • Clustering: detect + rm outliers.
  • Combined computer \(+\) human: machine flags suspicious, human checks.
Binning: 2 partitioning rules
  • Equal-width (distance): \(N\) intervals of equal size.
  • Equal-depth (frequency): \(N\) intervals, each with \(\approx\) same no. of samples. Better for skewed data.
Equal-width bin width, \(A =\) lowest value, \(B =\) highest, \(N =\) no. of bins: \[ W = \frac{B - A}{N} \] Your class notes print \(W=(A-B)/N\), which gives a negative width. Wrong: it is \((B-A)/N\). verified/added

column5: 74 Ash, 74 Ch

column4:
• Combines data from multiple sources into 1 coherent store.
  • Issues:
    • Entity identification: is cust_id in A the same as cust_no in B? Solved w/ metadata.
    • Redundancy: an attr derivable from another. Detect by correlation analysis (\(\chi^2\) for nominal, correlation coefficient \(+\) covariance for numeric).
    • Data value conflicts: same entity, diff values across sources (diff units, scales, currency, representation).
    • Duplication at tuple level.
  • Careful integration \(\rightarrow\) reduces/avoids redundancy \(\rightarrow\) improves mining speed + quality.
\(\chi^2\) test of independence (nominal pairs) NEW
  • \(H_0\): the 2 attrs are independent. \(H_1\): associated (so 1 is redundant).
  • Build the contingency table of observed counts \(O_{ij}\).
  • Expected count \(E_{ij} = \dfrac{(\text{row}_i\ \text{total})\times(\text{col}_j\ \text{total})} {\text{grand total}}\)
  • \(\chi^2 = \sum_{i,j} \dfrac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}\),   \(df = (r-1)(c-1)\).
  • \(\chi^2 >\) critical value at \(\alpha\) \(\rightarrow\) reject \(H_0\) \(\rightarrow\) correlated \(\rightarrow\) drop one attr.
Worked in one line
  • Gender (M/F) vs preference (like/dislike), 100 people, all 4 margins \(=50\).
  • Every \(E_{ij} = \frac{50\times 50}{100} = 25\). Observed 20/30/30/20.
  • \(\chi^2 = 4\times\frac{5^2}{25} = \mathbf{4}\), \(df = (2-1)(2-1) = 1\).
  • Critical value at \(\alpha = 0.05\), \(df=1\) is \(3.841\). \(4 > 3.841\) \(\rightarrow\) reject \(H_0\), gender and preference are associated.
  • Correlation \(\ne\) causation. Numeric analogue: \(r_{A,B} = \frac{Cov(A,B)}{\sigma_A\sigma_B}\), formula in §2.4.

column4:
Transformation methods
  • Smoothing: rm noise.
  • Aggregation: summarise, build data cube.
  • Generalisation: climb concept hierarchy (street \(\rightarrow\) city \(\rightarrow\) country).
  • Normalisation: scale into a small range.
  • Attribute construction: build new attrs from given ones.
Why normalise
  • Stops large-range attrs dominating small-range ones.
  • Required by distance-based methods: KNN, K-means, ANN.
The 3 normalisation formulas (memorise exactly)
1. Min-max \(\rightarrow\) maps to \([new\_min,\ new\_max]\): \[ v' = \frac{v - min_A}{max_A - min_A}\,(new\_max_A - new\_min_A) + new\_min_A \] 2. Z-score (zero-mean) \(\rightarrow\) use when min/max unknown or outliers present: \[ v' = \frac{v - \bar{A}}{\sigma_A} \qquad \bar{A}=\text{mean},\ \sigma_A=\text{std deviation} \] 3. Decimal scaling: \[ v' = \frac{v}{10^{\,j}} \quad j = \text{smallest int s.t. } \max(|v'|) < 1 \] Variant of 2: z-score w/ mean absolute deviation \(s_A\), more robust to outliers than \(\sigma_A\) (deviations are not squared): \[ s_A = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_i |v_i - \bar{A}| \qquad v' = \frac{v-\bar{A}}{s_A} \]
Error in your class notes verified/added : z-score is printed there as \(v' = (v - min)/\sigma\). That is wrong. It is \((v - \textbf{mean})/\sigma\). Using \(min\) makes every \(v'\ge 0\), which defeats the whole point of a zero-mean score.

  • Han & Kamber's 3-way split NEW (safer skeleton for a 5-mark answer):
    • Dimensionality reduction: wavelet transform, PCA, attribute subset selection. Fewer attributes.
    • Numerosity reduction: replace the data by a smaller representation. Fewer tuples.
      • Parametric: fit a model, store only its parameters \(\rightarrow\) regression, log-linear models.
      • Non-parametric: store a reduced form directly \(\rightarrow\) histograms, clustering, sampling, data cube aggregation.
    • Data compression: lossless (exact rebuild) vs lossy (approximation). The other two are themselves forms of compression.
Sampling types
  • Simple random: equal prob for each item.
  • W/o replacement: item removed once picked.
  • W/ replacement: not removed, same item can repeat.
  • Stratified: split into partitions, sample each. Best for skewed data.
The four forms at a glance
Cleaning, integration, reduction (attributes A1..A126 to A1..A115, tuples T1..T2000 to fewer), transformation (\(-2, 32, 100 \rightarrow -0.02, 0.32, 1.00\)). The one-figure answer to “forms of preprocessing”. H&K Fig 3.1.
Feature subset selection
  • Rm redundant features (purchase price + sales tax paid).
  • Rm irrelevant features (student ID for predicting GPA).
  • Techniques:
    • Brute force: try all subsets.
    • Embedded: selection happens inside the algorithm.
    • Filter: select before the algorithm runs.
    • Wrapper: use algorithm as a black box to score subsets.
Discretisation (feeds Ch 3 decision trees)
  • Continuous \(\rightarrow\) small no. of interval labels. Many algorithms need discrete input.
  • Unsupervised (no class labels):
    • Equal-width, equal-frequency, k-means (cluster values, 1 bin per cluster).
  • Supervised (uses class labels): entropy-based.
    • \(H(p_1,\dots,p_s) = \sum_i p_i \log_2(1/p_i) = -\sum_i p_i \log_2(p_i)\) same quantity as \(Info(D)\) in Ch 3, §3.2 — written both ways in the literature
    • Split \(S\) at boundary \(T\): \(E(S,T) = \frac{|S_1|}{|S|}Ent(S_1) + \frac{|S_2|}{|S|}Ent(S_2)\)
    • Pick \(T\) minimising \(E\); recurse until \(Ent(S)-E(T,S) \le \delta\).
  • Also: mapping to a new space (Fourier, wavelet transform).

• As dims \(\uparrow\), data becomes increasingly sparse in the space it occupies.
  • Density + distance lose meaning \(\rightarrow\) breaks clustering + outlier detection.
  • All points start looking equidistant.

column4:
Key idea
  • Find a projection capturing the largest variance in the data.
  • New axes \(=\) eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by eigenvalue.
  • Eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) \(=\) variance carried by principal component \(i\).
  • Keep the top \(r\) components \(\rightarrow\) drop the rest w/ little info loss.
  • Components are orthogonal (uncorrelated).
Proportion of variance explained
\[ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i} = \frac{\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_r}{\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_m} \]
  • Denominator \(=\) trace of covariance matrix \(=\) total variance.
PCA process: 5 steps (DBK's sequence)
  1. Subtract the mean from each dimension \(\rightarrow\) zero-mean data.
  2. Compute the covariance matrix.
  3. Compute eigenvalues + eigenvectors of that matrix.
  4. Choose components, form feature vector: sort \(\lambda\) descending, keep top \(r\), put their eigenvectors in columns.
  5. Derive new data: FinalData = RowFeatureVector \(\times\) RowZeroMeanData.
Notes
  • Eigenvectors exist only for square matrices.
  • An \(m\times m\) matrix gives \(m\) of them.
  • Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix are mutually perpendicular.
  • Normalise eigenvectors to unit length.
  • Highly correlated dims \(\rightarrow\) few large \(\lambda\) \(\rightarrow\) PCA helps a lot. Uncorrelated dims \(\rightarrow\) \(r\approx m\) \(\rightarrow\) PCA does not help.
Error in your class notes verified/added : the PCA section there lists “construct a neighbourhood graph” and “compute shortest-path / geodesic distances”. Those steps belong to Isomap, a non-linear method, not PCA. PCA is purely linear: covariance \(\rightarrow\) eigenvectors.

column1: Explain typical OLAP operations over a multidim DW. Differentiate OLAP vs OLTP.
column4:
Multidimensional model
  • Dimension: perspective the org keeps records by. Eg time, item, location, branch.
  • Measure: the numeric quantity analysed. Eg units_sold, dollars_sold.
  • Fact table: stores measures \(+\) FKs to dimension tables.
  • Data cube: lets you view measures against a set of dims.
  • Cuboid: the cube at one level of summarisation.
    • Base cuboid \(=\) lowest level, all \(n\) dims.
    • Apex cuboid \(=\) 0-D, highest summary, denoted all.
    • Lattice of cuboids \(=\) the full cube. \(n\) dims \(\rightarrow\) \(2^n\) cuboids.
  • Schemas: star, snowflake, fact constellation \(\rightarrow\) defined in Ch 1.
  • Concept hierarchy: the levels of abstraction inside 1 dim, eg street \(<\) city \(<\) province \(<\) country.
    • This is what roll-up and drill-down actually climb.
    • Supplied manually by users/experts, or generated automatically from the data distribution.
3 kinds of measure, by aggregate function
  • Distributive: partition the data, aggregate each part, aggregate the results \(\rightarrow\) same answer. sum(), count(), min(), max().
  • Algebraic: computable from a bounded no. of distributive functions. avg() = sum()/count(), min_N(), standard_deviation().
  • Holistic: no constant-size sub-aggregate suffices. median(), mode(), rank(). Expensive \(\rightarrow\) usually estimated.
The 5 OLAP operations (the core answer)
  • Roll-up (drill-up): summarise by climbing a hierarchy or reducing a dim. Eg city \(\rightarrow\) country; or drop time entirely.
  • Drill-down (roll-down): reverse of roll-up. Summary \(\rightarrow\) detail, or introduce a new dim. Eg quarter \(\rightarrow\) month.
  • Slice: select on one dim \(\rightarrow\) sub-cube. Eg time = Q1.
  • Dice: select on two or more dims. Eg location in {Kathmandu, Pokhara} and time in {Q1,Q2}.
  • Pivot (rotate): rotate axes to give an alternative presentation. 3-D \(\rightarrow\) series of 2-D planes.
  • Others: drill-across (across \(\ge\)2 fact tables), drill-through (down to the back-end relational tables).
OLAP vs OLTP (asked 4 times)
  • Users: OLTP clerks / IT \(\cdot\) OLAP knowledge workers.
  • Function: OLTP day-to-day ops \(\cdot\) OLAP decision support.
  • DB design: OLTP application-oriented, normalised (ER) \(\cdot\) OLAP subject-oriented, de-normalised (star/snowflake).
  • Data: OLTP current, detailed, isolated \(\cdot\) OLAP historical, summarised, multidim, consolidated.
  • Usage: OLTP repetitive \(\cdot\) OLAP ad-hoc.
  • Access: OLTP read/write, index on primary key \(\cdot\) OLAP lots of scans.
  • Unit of work: OLTP short simple txn \(\cdot\) OLAP complex query.
  • Records accessed: tens \(\cdot\) millions.
  • Size: 100 MB–GB \(\cdot\) 100 GB–TB.
  • Metric: txn throughput \(\cdot\) query throughput / response.
OLAP server types (detail in Ch 1, DW architecture)
  • ROLAP: relational back end. Scales best.
  • MOLAP: multidim array store. Fastest, wastes space on sparse data.
  • HOLAP: hybrid. Detail relational \(+\) aggregates multidim.

column1: How is similarity/dissimilarity calculated? Properties of a distance metric.
column4:
Similarity vs dissimilarity
  • Similarity: how alike 2 objects are. Higher \(=\) more alike. Usually \([0,1]\).
  • Dissimilarity / distance: how different. Lower \(=\) more alike. Min \(=0\), upper limit varies, often \([0,\infty]\).
  • Used for: clustering, KNN, outlier detection, search, recommendation, near-duplicate detection.
Distance metric: 4 properties (71 Ch asks exactly this, 10)
  1. Non-negativity: \(d(x,y) \ge 0\).
  2. Identity: \(d(x,y) = 0\) iff \(x = y\).
  3. Symmetry: \(d(x,y) = d(y,x)\).
  4. Triangle inequality: \(d(x,y) \le d(x,z) + d(z,y)\).
  • Triangle inequality \(\rightarrow\) guarantees the function is well behaved: the direct connection is the shortest.
  • A measure satisfying all 4 \(=\) a metric. Minkowski distances are metrics for \(r\ge1\).
  • Subtle point worth 1 mark: non-negativity is implied by the other 3, so strictly only 3 are independent.
  • Weighted Euclidean (attrs of unequal importance): \(d(i,j)=\sqrt{\sum_k w_k (x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2}\).
Minkowski family: the one formula that generates the rest
\(\displaystyle dist(p,q) = \Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n} |p_k - q_k|^{\,r}\Big)^{1/r}\)
  • \(n\) \(=\) no. of dims, \(r\) \(=\) parameter, \(r \ge 1\). Do not confuse \(r\) with \(n\).
  • Notation clash: H&K call the parameter \(h\) and reserve \(p\) for the no. of attrs; other books write \(L_p\) where their \(p\) is this \(r\). Define your symbols.
  • \(r=1\) \(\rightarrow\) Manhattan (\(L_1\), city block, taxicab). Binary case \(=\) Hamming distance.
  • \(r=2\) \(\rightarrow\) Euclidean (\(L_2\)).
  • \(r\rightarrow\infty\) \(\rightarrow\) Supremum (\(L_{max}\), \(L_\infty\), Chebyshev, chessboard) \(=\) max difference in any single coordinate.
Written out
  • Euclidean: \(\sqrt{\sum_k (p_k-q_k)^2}\)
  • Manhattan: \(\sum_k |p_k - q_k|\)
  • Supremum: \(\max_k |p_k - q_k|\)
Binary attributes: SMC vs Jaccard 2+2+2
Build a \(2\times2\) contingency count for objects \(i,j\). Two notations exist, know both:
  • \(q = M_{11}\) \(=\) attrs where both \(=1\)   \(t = M_{00}\) \(=\) attrs where both \(=0\)
  • \(r = M_{10}\) \(=\) \(i{=}1,\,j{=}0\)    \(s = M_{01}\) \(=\) \(i{=}0,\,j{=}1\)
  • Total \(p = q+r+s+t\). H&K use \(q,r,s,t\); Tan and DBK use \(M_{11}\) etc.
\[ \underbrace{d = \frac{r+s}{q+r+s+t}}_{\textbf{symmetric}} \qquad \underbrace{d = \frac{r+s}{q+r+s}}_{\textbf{asymmetric}} \qquad \underbrace{SMC = \frac{q+t}{q+r+s+t}}_{=\,1-d_{sym}} \qquad \underbrace{J = \frac{q}{q+r+s}}_{=\,1-d_{asym}} \]
  • Only difference: Jaccard/asymmetric drop \(t\) (the 0-0 matches).
  • SMC \(\rightarrow\) symmetric binary (a 0-0 match is informative).
  • Jaccard \(\rightarrow\) asymmetric binary (0-0 meaningless: 2 people both lacking a rare disease says nothing).
  • Sets form: \(J(A,B) = |A\cap B| / |A\cup B|\).
  • Read the verb. “Find the Jaccard coefficient” wants \(J\); “find the dissimilarity” wants \(d = 1-J\).
Nominal attributes
\[ d(i,j) = \frac{p-m}{p} \qquad sim(i,j) = 1-d(i,j) = \frac{m}{p} \]
  • \(m\) \(=\) no. of attrs where \(i\) and \(j\) are in the same state, \(p\) \(=\) total attrs.
  • Alternative: encode each of the \(M\) states as an asymmetric binary attr, then use Jaccard.
Ordinal attributes
  1. Replace value \(x_{if}\) by its rank \(r_{if} \in \{1,\dots,M_f\}\).
  2. Normalise rank to \([0,1]\) so every attr has equal weight: \[ z_{if} = \frac{r_{if}-1}{M_f-1} \]
  3. Treat \(z_{if}\) as numeric \(\rightarrow\) use Euclidean / Manhattan.
  • Eg {fair, good, excellent}, \(M_f=3\) \(\rightarrow\) ranks 1,2,3 \(\rightarrow\) \(z = 0,\ 0.5,\ 1\).
Data matrix vs dissimilarity matrix
  • Data matrix (\(n\) objects \(\times\) \(p\) attrs): stores the objects themselves. Two-mode (rows \(=\) objects, cols \(=\) attrs).
  • Dissimilarity matrix (\(n\times n\)): stores \(d(i,j)\) for every pair. One-mode (both axes are objects).
  • Properties: \(d(i,i)=0\), \(d(i,j)=d(j,i)\) \(\rightarrow\) only the lower triangle is written.
  • Most clustering + KNN algorithms run on the dissimilarity matrix.
Mixed attribute types
\[ d(i,j) = \frac{\sum_{f=1}^{p}\delta_{ij}^{(f)} d_{ij}^{(f)}}{\sum_{f=1}^{p}\delta_{ij}^{(f)}} \]
  • \(\delta_{ij}^{(f)}=0\) if the attr is missing for either object, or it is asymmetric binary and both are 0. Else \(\delta = 1\).
  • \(d_{ij}^{(f)}\) computed per attr type, each scaled to \([0,1]\) (numeric: divide by the range).
Cosine similarity 3
\[ \cos(d_1,d_2) = \frac{d_1 \cdot d_2}{\lVert d_1\rVert\,\lVert d_2\rVert} \]
  • \(d_1\cdot d_2 =\) dot product, \(\lVert d\rVert = \sqrt{\sum d_k^2}\) \(=\) vector length.
  • Range \([0,1]\) for non-negative vectors.
  • Aligned \(\rightarrow\) angle \(0^\circ\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\cos=1\). Orthogonal (no common terms) \(\rightarrow\) \(90^\circ\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\cos=0\).
  • Ignores magnitude, measures direction only \(\rightarrow\) ideal for documents, where doc length shouldnt matter.
Correlation coefficient
\[ corr(x,y) = \frac{\sum_i (x_i-\mu_x)(y_i-\mu_y)} {\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i-\mu_x)^2}\sqrt{\sum_i (y_i-\mu_y)^2}} = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_x s_y} \]
  • \(=\) cosine similarity of the mean-centred vectors.
  • Range \([-1,1]\): \(+1\) positive, \(-1\) negative, \(0\) no correlation.
  • Covariance \(s_{xy} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_k (x_k-\bar{x})(y_k-\bar{y})\).
  • Correlation \(=\) scaled (unit-free) version of covariance.
Which measure for which data (picking wrong = losing the marks)
DataUse
Numeric, scale mattersEuclidean / Manhattan / Minkowski
Numeric, only direction matters (documents)Cosine
Symmetric binarySMC
Asymmetric binary, setsJaccard
Nominal / categoricalSimple mismatch \(d = (p-m)/p\), \(m=\) no. of matches, \(p=\) total attrs
StringsHamming (equal length) / Levenshtein edit distance
Testing linear relationshipCorrelation coefficient

Method
  • Min-max maps \(v\) into \([new\_min,\ new\_max]\), preserves relationships exactly: \[ v' = \frac{v - min_A}{max_A - min_A}(new\_max_A - new\_min_A) + new\_min_A \]
  • Z-score uses mean \(\bar{A}\) and std deviation \(\sigma_A\). Use when min/max unknown, or outliers would squash a min-max result: \[ v' = \frac{v - \bar{A}}{\sigma_A} \qquad \sigma_A = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum (v_i-\bar{A})^2} \]
  • Decimal scaling moves the decimal point: \[ v' = \frac{v}{10^{\,j}}, \quad j = \text{smallest int such that } \max(|v'|) < 1 \]
Two traps. (1) Z-score uses the mean, not the min. (2) For decimal scaling, \(j\) must make the max strictly less than 1, so \(\max|v|=1000\) needs \(j=4\), not \(j=3\).

column1: M2. PCA: principal components and proportion of variance
column4:
Method
  1. Start from the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) (if given raw data: subtract the mean first, then compute \(\Sigma\)).
  2. Solve the characteristic equation \(|\Sigma - \lambda I| = 0\) for the eigenvalues \(\lambda\).
  3. Sort \(\lambda\) in descending order. \(\lambda_i\) \(=\) variance carried by component \(i\).
  4. For each \(\lambda_i\) solve \((\Sigma - \lambda_i I)\,\mathbf{v} = 0\) for the eigenvector, then normalise it to unit length.
  5. Proportion of total variance explained by component \(i\): \[ \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_j \lambda_j}, \qquad \sum_j\lambda_j = \text{trace}(\Sigma) \]
  • Check: the eigenvalues must sum to the trace. Free and catches arithmetic slips.
column7: M2. PCA: principal components and proportion of variance

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Chaitra · Q1 · [4]
Find the principal components and the proportion of the total variance explained by each when the covariance matrix of the three random variables \(X_1\), \(X_2\) and \(X_3\) is: \[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \]
column4:
Step 1: characteristic equation
  • The third row/column is decoupled, so \(\Sigma\) splits into a \(2\times2\) block and a \(1\times1\) block.
  • From the \(1\times1\) block: \((2-\lambda) = 0 \Rightarrow \boxed{\lambda = 2}\)
  • From the \(2\times2\) block: \[ (1-\lambda)(5-\lambda) - (-2)(-2) = 0 \] \[ 5 - 6\lambda + \lambda^2 - 4 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 1 = 0 \] \[ \lambda = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36-4}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{32}}{2} = 3 \pm 2\sqrt{2} \]
Step 2: eigenvalues, sorted
  • \(\lambda_1 = 3 + 2\sqrt{2} = \mathbf{5.8284}\)
  • \(\lambda_2 = \mathbf{2}\)
  • \(\lambda_3 = 3 - 2\sqrt{2} = \mathbf{0.1716}\)
  • Check: \(5.8284 + 2 + 0.1716 = 8 = \) trace\((\Sigma) = 1+5+2\). Correct.
Step 3: eigenvectors
  • For \(\lambda_1 = 5.8284\): row 1 gives \((1-5.8284)v_1 - 2v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = -2.4142\,v_1\); row 3 gives \(v_3=0\).
    \(\mathbf{e}_1 \propto (1,\ -2.4142,\ 0)\), length \(\sqrt{1+5.8284}=2.6131\)
    \(\mathbf{e}_1 = (0.3827,\ -0.9239,\ 0)\)
  • For \(\lambda_2 = 2\): rows 1 and 2 force \(v_1=v_2=0\), \(v_3\) free.
    \(\mathbf{e}_2 = (0,\ 0,\ 1)\)
  • For \(\lambda_3 = 0.1716\): row 1 gives \(0.8284\,v_1 = 2v_2 \Rightarrow v_2 = 0.4142\,v_1\); \(v_3=0\).
    \(\mathbf{e}_3 \propto (1,\ 0.4142,\ 0)\), length \(1.0824\)
    \(\mathbf{e}_3 = (0.9239,\ 0.3827,\ 0)\)
  • Check: \(\mathbf{e}_1\cdot\mathbf{e}_3 = (0.3827)(0.9239)+(-0.9239)(0.3827) = 0\) \(\rightarrow\) orthogonal, as required for a symmetric matrix.
Step 4: proportion of variance
PC\(\lambda_i\)\(\lambda_i/8\)
PC15.8284\(\mathbf{72.86\%}\)
PC22.0000\(\mathbf{25.00\%}\)
PC30.1716\(\mathbf{2.14\%}\)
Total8.0000100%
Interpretation
  • PC1 alone carries \(\approx\)73% of the variance.
  • PC1 \(+\) PC2 carry \(\mathbf{97.86\%}\) \(\rightarrow\) dropping PC3 loses only \(2.14\%\).
  • So 3 dims reduce to 2 with almost no information loss.
Final answer
  • PC1: \(\lambda_1 = 5.8284\), \(\mathbf{e}_1 = (0.3827, -0.9239, 0)\), 72.86%
  • PC2: \(\lambda_2 = 2\), \(\mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 0, 1)\), 25.00%
  • PC3: \(\lambda_3 = 0.1716\), \(\mathbf{e}_3 = (0.9239, 0.3827, 0)\), 2.14%

column1: M3. Distance measures and the distance matrix
column4:
Method
  • All three are Minkowski with a different \(r\): \[ dist(p,q) = \Big(\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}|p_k-q_k|^{\,r}\Big)^{1/r} \]
  • \(r=1\) Manhattan: \(\sum|p_k-q_k|\)
  • \(r=2\) Euclidean: \(\sqrt{\sum(p_k-q_k)^2}\)
  • \(r\to\infty\) Supremum (\(L_\infty\), Chebyshev): \(\max_k|p_k-q_k|\)
  • A distance matrix is symmetric with a zero diagonal, so only the lower triangle needs computing.

Method
\[ \cos(d_1,d_2) = \frac{d_1\cdot d_2}{\lVert d_1\rVert\,\lVert d_2\rVert}, \qquad d_1\cdot d_2 = \sum_k d_{1k}d_{2k}, \qquad \lVert d\rVert = \sqrt{\sum_k d_k^2} \]

Method

    • \(M_{10}\): \(p=1,q=0\)   \(M_{01}\): \(p=0,q=1\)

  • Symmetric binary dissimilarity: \(\displaystyle d = \frac{M_{10}+M_{01}}{M_{11}+M_{00}+M_{10}+M_{01}} = 1 - SMC\)
  • Nominal (non-binary) dissimilarity: \(d = (p-m)/p\), \(m =\) matches, \(p =\) total attrs.

  1. Put the measures in a central fact table, plus one foreign key per dimension.
  2. Draw one dimension table per dimension around it.
    • Star \(\rightarrow\) leave dimension tables flat (de-normalised).
    • Snowflake \(\rightarrow\) normalise the hierarchies into sub-tables (location \(\rightarrow\) city \(\rightarrow\) province).
  3. For the OLAP sequence, work from the base cuboid and ask, per dimension:
    • Need a coarser level? \(\rightarrow\) roll-up
    • Need a finer level? \(\rightarrow\) drill-down
    • Restricting 1 dimension? \(\rightarrow\) slice. Restricting \(\ge\)2? \(\rightarrow\) dice
    • Dimension not wanted at all? \(\rightarrow\) roll-up to all (dimension reduction)
  4. \(n\) dimensions \(\rightarrow\) \(2^n\) cuboids in the lattice.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2078 Bhadra · Q2 · [3+3]
Suppose that a data warehouse consists of the four dimensions data, spectator, location, and game, and the two measures count and charge, where charge is the fare that a spectator pays when watching a game on a given date. Spectators may be students, adults or seniors, with each category having its own charge rate.
  1. Draw a star schema diagram for the data warehouse.
  2. Starting with the base cuboid [data, spectator, location, game], what specific OLAP operations should you perform in order to list the total charge paid by student spectators at Dashrath Stadium in 2021?
column4:
(a) Star schema
  • Fact table Sales: date_key, spectator_key, location_key, game_key, count, charge.
  • Dimension tables (flat, one hop from the fact table):
    • date(date_key, day, month, quarter, year)
    • spectator(spectator_key, name, status, phone, address) where status \(\in\) {student, adult, senior}
    • location(location_key, name, street, city, province, country)
    • game(game_key, name, description, sport_type)
  • 4 dimensions \(\rightarrow\) \(2^4 = \mathbf{16}\) cuboids in the lattice.
(b) OLAP operation sequence
  1. Roll-up on date from date_key to year.
  2. Roll-up on spectator from spectator_key to status.
  3. Roll-up on location from location_key to location_name.
  4. Roll-up on game to all (the question does not split by game).
  5. Dice with year = 2021 and status = student and location_name = “Dashrath Stadium”.
  6. Read off the charge measure (summed).
  • Dice, not slice \(\rightarrow\) 3 dimensions are being restricted at once.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Chaitra · Q3 · [3+3]
Suppose that a data warehouse for a sales company consists of five dimensions: time, location, supplier, brand, and product, and two measures: count and price.
  1. Draw a snowflake schema diagram for the data warehouse.
  2. Starting with the base cuboid [time, location, supplier, brand, product], what specific OLAP operations should one perform in order to list the total count for a certain brand for each state per year (assume location has three levels: country, state, city; and assume time has three levels: year, month, day)?
column4:
(a) Snowflake schema
  • Fact table Sales: time_key, location_key, supplier_key, brand_key, product_key, count, price.
  • Normalised hierarchies (this is what makes it a snowflake, not a star):
    • time(time_key, day, month_key) \(\rightarrow\) month(month_key, month, year)
    • location(location_key, city_key) \(\rightarrow\) city(city_key, city, state_key) \(\rightarrow\) state(state_key, state, country)
    • product(product_key, name, brand_key) \(\rightarrow\) brand(brand_key, brand_name)
    • supplier(supplier_key, supplier_name, supplier_type)
  • 5 dimensions \(\rightarrow\) \(2^5 = \mathbf{32}\) cuboids.
(b) OLAP operation sequence
  1. Roll-up on time from day to year.
  2. Roll-up on location from city to state.
  3. Roll-up on supplier to all (not wanted).
  4. Roll-up on product to brand level.
  5. Slice on brand = the given brand (1 dimension restricted).
  6. Result: cuboid [year, state] holding total count.

column1: M7. Central tendency, quartiles, IQR and outliers
column4:
Method
  • Grouped median \(= L_1 + \left(\dfrac{N/2 - (\sum freq)_l}{freq_{median}}\right)\times width\). Find the median interval first: the one where cumulative frequency first reaches \(N/2\).
  • Mode from mean and median \(\approx 3\,median - 2\,mean\) (unimodal, moderately skewed).
  • Quartiles, interpolated convention: position of \(Q_k = \frac{k(n+1)}{4}\), then interpolate between the neighbouring sorted values.
  • Outlier fences: below \(Q_1 - 1.5\,IQR\) or above \(Q_3 + 1.5\,IQR\).

column1: Problem 7.3 — mode from mean and median
column3:
PROBLEM not a PYQ · PC's notes · [2]
For a unimodal, moderately skewed distribution the mean is 60 and the median is 55. Estimate the mode, and state what the result says about the skew.
column4:
• \(mean - mode \approx 3(mean - median) \Rightarrow mode \approx 3\,median - 2\,mean\).
  • \(mode \approx 3(55) - 2(60) = 165 - 120 = \mathbf{45}\).
  • Sanity check: \(mode < median < mean \rightarrow\) positively skewed. Consistent.

column1: Problem 7.4 — full descriptive summary of one dataset
column3:
PROBLEM not a PYQ · Han & Kamber Example 2.6 · [2+2+2+2]
Suppose that the data for analysis is the salaries (in $1000s) of 12 employees, already sorted in increasing order: \[ 30,\ 36,\ 47,\ 50,\ 52,\ 52,\ 56,\ 60,\ 63,\ 70,\ 70,\ 110 \] Find (a) the mean, median and mode; (b) the quartiles \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) and the IQR; (c) the five-number summary; (d) any outliers using the \(1.5\times IQR\) rule.
column4:
(a) Central tendency
  • \(\sum x = 696 \rightarrow mean = \frac{696}{12} = \mathbf{58}\).
  • \(n\) even \(\rightarrow median = \frac{52+56}{2} = \mathbf{54}\).
  • 52 and 70 each occur twice \(\rightarrow\) bimodal, modes \(\mathbf{52}\) and \(\mathbf{70}\).
  • \(midrange = \frac{30+110}{2} = \mathbf{70}\).
  • \(mode < median < mean\) is broken here by the bimodality; the single outlier 110 is what pulls the mean above the median.
(b) Quartiles, positional convention (Han & Kamber)
  • Take the 3rd, 6th, 9th sorted values \(\rightarrow Q_1 = 47\), \(Q_2 = 52\), \(Q_3 = 63\).
  • \(IQR = 63 - 47 = \mathbf{16}\).
(c) Quartiles, interpolated convention (PC's class notes)
  • \(Q_1\) at \(\frac{1(13)}{4} = 3.25 \rightarrow 47 + 0.25(50-47) = \mathbf{47.75}\)
  • \(Q_2\) at \(\frac{2(13)}{4} = 6.5 \ \rightarrow 52 + 0.5(56-52) = \mathbf{54}\)
  • \(Q_3\) at \(\frac{3(13)}{4} = 9.75 \rightarrow 63 + 0.75(70-63) = \mathbf{68.25}\)
  • \(IQR = 68.25 - 47.75 = \mathbf{20.5}\)
(d) Five-number summary and outliers
  • Five-number summary (interpolated): \(\mathbf{30,\ 47.75,\ 54,\ 68.25,\ 110}\).
  • Fences: \(47.75 - 1.5(20.5) = 17.0\) and \(68.25 + 1.5(20.5) = 99.0\).
  • \(110 > 99 \rightarrow \mathbf{110}\) is a suspected outlier. Nothing below 17.
  • Cross-check with the other convention: fences \(47 - 24 = 23\) and \(63 + 24 = 87\). 110 is still the only outlier \(\rightarrow\) the verdict does not depend on the convention, so either is safe in the exam as long as you name it.
(e) Boxplot
  • Box from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\), line at 54, whiskers to 30 and to the largest non-outlier (70), and 110 plotted as a lone point.
Drawn to scale by boxfig.py from the values above. The whisker stops at 70, not at the fence.

The following price data has already been sorted: \[ 4,\ 8,\ 9,\ 15,\ 21,\ 21,\ 24,\ 25,\ 26,\ 28,\ 29,\ 34 \] Partition the data into equal-depth bins of depth 4, then smooth the noise by (i) bin means and (ii) bin boundaries.

Solution
  • 12 values, depth 4 \(\rightarrow\) 3 bins.

    • Bin 1 mean \(= 36/4 = 9\) \(\rightarrow\) 9, 9, 9, 9
    • Bin 2 mean \(= 91/4 = 22.75 \approx 23\) \(\rightarrow\) 23, 23, 23, 23
    • Bin 3 mean \(= 117/4 = 29.25 \approx 29\) \(\rightarrow\) 29, 29, 29, 29
  • (ii) Smoothing by bin boundaries (each value \(\rightarrow\) nearer of min/max)
    • Bin 1 (min 4, max 15): 4, 8, 9, 15 \(\rightarrow\) 4, 4, 4, 15 (8 and 9 are nearer 4)
    • Bin 2 (min 21, max 25): 21, 21, 24, 25 \(\rightarrow\) 21, 21, 25, 25
    • Bin 3 (min 26, max 34): 26, 28, 29, 34 \(\rightarrow\) 26, 26, 26, 34

column1: Why is classification a supervised learning method?
column4:
Classification
  • Predicts categorical class labels (discrete, nominal).
  • Supervised: the training tuples come w/ a known class label. The model learns from labelled answers.
  • vs unsupervised (clustering): no labels given, groups discovered. \(\rightarrow\) Ch 5
  • vs prediction / regression: predicts a continuous value, not a label.
2-step process (this is the block diagram Q)
  1. Learning / model construction (training)
    • Input: training set, each tuple w/ its class label.
    • Output: the model, as rules / tree / formula.
  2. Classification / model usage (testing then deployment)
    • Estimate accuracy on an independent test set.
    • Test set must be separate from the training set, else the accuracy is optimistic (the model has memorised).
    • If accuracy acceptable \(\rightarrow\) classify new, unlabelled data.
Where each classifier fits
  • Eager learners build the model before seeing a query: decision tree, Bayes, ANN, rule-based, SVM.
  • Lazy learners store the data and act only at query time: KNN, case-based.
Applications
  • Credit / loan approval, fraud detection, medical diagnosis, target marketing, churn prediction, spam filtering.
Answer skeleton 10
  1. Definition \(+\) “supervised because labels are given”.
  2. Draw the 2-step block diagram (training \(\rightarrow\) model \(\rightarrow\) testing \(\rightarrow\) deployment).
  3. Name the classifiers, 1 line each.
  4. Close w/ the 2–3 metrics used to judge one.
The 2-step block diagram, drawn
(a) Learning: labelled training data \(\rightarrow\) classification algorithm \(\rightarrow\) model (here as IF-THEN rules). (b) Classification: the rules are checked on a separate test set, then applied to a new tuple (John Henry \(\rightarrow\) risky). H&K Fig 8.1.

column1: What is a decision tree? How is information gain used for attribute selection?
column4:
Structure
  • Flow-chart-like inverted tree.
  • Root node: topmost, the first test.
  • Internal node: a test on one attribute.
  • Branch: an outcome of that test.
  • Leaf node: holds a class label.
  • Path root \(\rightarrow\) leaf \(=\) one classification rule.
Why popular
  • No domain knowledge or parameter setting needed.
  • Handles high-dimensional data.
  • Human-readable \(\rightarrow\) easy to convert to IF-THEN rules.
  • Fast; good accuracy in most cases.
Hunt's algorithm 72 Ka 10 \(\rightarrow\) the ancestor of all of them
Let \(D_t\) \(=\) training records reaching node \(t\), \(y=\{y_1\dots y_c\}\) the class labels.
  1. If all records in \(D_t\) belong to the same class \(y_t\) \(\rightarrow\) \(t\) is a leaf labelled \(y_t\).
  2. If \(D_t\) is empty \(\rightarrow\) leaf labelled w/ the majority class of the parent.
  3. If \(D_t\) has records of more than 1 class \(\rightarrow\) pick an attribute test, split \(D_t\) into subsets, recurse on each subset.
  • Descendants: ID3 \(\rightarrow\) C4.5 \(\rightarrow\) C5.0 (Quinlan), CART, SLIQ, SPRINT.
Generic induction algorithm
  • Greedy, top-down, recursive, divide-and-conquer.
  • Greedy \(=\) picks the locally best attribute at each node, never backtracks.
  • Stopping conditions:
    • all tuples at the node share 1 class, or
    • no attributes left \(\rightarrow\) leaf \(=\) majority class, or
    • no tuples left \(\rightarrow\) leaf \(=\) majority class of parent.
Test conditions per attribute type 72 Ka asks this
  • Binary: 2 outcomes, forced.
  • Nominal
    • Multi-way: 1 branch per value.
    • Binary: split values into 2 subsets. \(2^{v-1}-1\) ways.
  • Ordinal: same as nominal, but a grouping must not break the order.
  • Continuous
    • Binary: test \(A \le t\) vs \(A > t\).
    • Multi-way: discretise into ranges first.
    • Split point: sort values, try the midpoint of each adjacent pair, \(\frac{a_i + a_{i+1}}{2}\); \(v\) values \(\rightarrow\) \(v-1\) candidate splits. Pick the one w/ minimum \(Info_A(D)\).
The 3 attribute selection measures (memorise all three)
1. Information gain  ID3  maximise
\[ Info(D) = -\sum_{i=1}^{m} p_i \log_2 (p_i) \] \[ Info_A(D) = \sum_{j=1}^{v}\frac{|D_j|}{|D|}\times Info(D_j) \] \[ Gain(A) = Info(D) - Info_A(D) \]
  • \(p_i = |C_{i,D}|/|D|\) \(=\) fraction of class \(i\). \(Info(D)\) \(=\) entropy, in bits.
  • Pick the attribute w/ the highest \(Gain\).
  • Bias: prefers attrs w/ many distinct values (a unique ID gives \(Info_A=0\), so maximal gain, yet is useless).
2. Gain ratio  C4.5  maximise
\[ SplitInfo_A(D) = -\sum_{j=1}^{v}\frac{|D_j|}{|D|}\log_2\!\Big(\frac{|D_j|}{|D|}\Big) \] \[ GainRatio(A) = \frac{Gain(A)}{SplitInfo_A(D)} \]
  • Normalises the gain \(\rightarrow\) fixes the many-values bias.
  • Unstable as \(SplitInfo \rightarrow 0\); constrain \(Gain\) to be at least the average.
3. Gini index  CART  minimise
\[ Gini(D) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{m} p_i^{\,2} \] \[ Gini_A(D) = \frac{|D_1|}{|D|}Gini(D_1) + \frac{|D_2|}{|D|}Gini(D_2) \] \[ \Delta Gini(A) = Gini(D) - Gini_A(D) \]
  • Gini considers only BINARY splits \(\rightarrow\) for \(v\) values, try all \(2^{v-1}-1\) subset splits and keep the best.
  • Pick the attribute w/ the largest \(\Delta Gini\) (equivalently smallest \(Gini_A\)).
  • Bias: toward attrs w/ many values, and toward equal-sized balanced partitions.
Reading the measures
  • All 3 measure impurity. Pure node \(\rightarrow\) \(Info=0\), \(Gini=0\).
  • Max impurity: 2 classes 50/50 \(\rightarrow\) \(Info=1\), \(Gini=0.5\).
Advantages
  • Simple, fast to build and to apply.
  • Self-explanatory, converts directly to rules.
  • No normalisation or scaling needed.
  • Handles both nominal and numeric attrs, and irrelevant attrs.
Disadvantages
  • Greedy \(\rightarrow\) locally optimal, not guaranteed globally optimal.
  • Prone to overfitting without pruning.
  • Unstable: a small data change can restructure the whole tree.
  • Axis-parallel splits only \(\rightarrow\) struggles w/ diagonal boundaries.
  • Biased toward attrs w/ many values (unless gain ratio used).

• Tree grows branches that fit noise and outliers \(\rightarrow\) poor accuracy on new data.
  • Pre-pruning (early stopping)
    • Halt splitting at a node; make it a leaf w/ the majority class.
    • Stop if: gain below a threshold, too few tuples, purity high enough.

  • Post-pruning (grow full, then cut) \(\rightarrow\) preferred
    • Remove subtrees from a fully grown tree, replace w/ a leaf.

    • C4.5 uses pessimistic pruning, no extra data needed.
  • Other fixes: more training data, cross-validation, ensembles.

column1: How does a Rule Based Classifier work? Explain with example.
column4:
Form
  • Model \(=\) a set of IF-THEN rules.
  • IF (age = youth) AND (student = yes) THEN buys_computer = yes
  • Antecedent (LHS, the condition) \(\rightarrow\) Consequent (RHS, the class).
  • A rule covers a tuple if the antecedent holds; the rule is then said to be triggered.
Rule quality measures 70 Ch asks Accuracy + Laplace verified/added
  • \(n_{covers}\) \(=\) tuples covered by \(R\), \(n_{correct}\) \(=\) those it labels correctly, \(|D|\) \(=\) size of the data set, \(k\) \(=\) no. of classes.
\[ Coverage(R) = \frac{n_{covers}}{|D|} \qquad Accuracy(R) = \frac{n_{correct}}{n_{covers}} \] \[ Laplace(R) = \frac{n_{correct}+1}{n_{covers}+k} \qquad m\text{-}estimate(R) = \frac{n_{correct}+k\,p}{n_{covers}+k} \]
  • Why Laplace: plain accuracy rates a rule covering 1 tuple correctly as \(1.0\), which is meaningless. Laplace pulls small-coverage rules toward the prior, so a rule must cover enough tuples to score well.
  • Eg 1 tuple, 1 correct, 2 classes: \(Accuracy = 1/1 = 1.0\) but \(Laplace = 2/3 = 0.67\).
Conflict resolution 76 Ch 2+4
  • Why needed: a tuple may trigger several rules predicting different classes, or no rule at all.
  • Size ordering (rule antecedent size): the most specific rule wins, ie the one w/ the most attribute tests. Intuition: more conditions \(=\) more evidence.
  • Class-based ordering: classes sorted by decreasing prevalence (or by misclassification cost). All rules of one class come as a block.
  • Rule-based ordering (decision list): rules ranked by quality (accuracy, coverage, size) by the expert or the algorithm. First rule that fires wins.
  • No rule fires \(\rightarrow\) use a default rule, predicting the majority class of the tuples not covered by any rule. Always placed last.
Two useful properties
  • Mutually exclusive: no 2 rules fire on the same tuple \(\rightarrow\) no conflict possible.
  • Exhaustive: every possible tuple is covered \(\rightarrow\) no default rule needed.
  • Rules extracted from a decision tree are both by construction.
Rule extraction from a decision tree
  • 1 rule per root-to-leaf path. Each split condition ANDed; leaf \(=\) consequent.
  • Mutually exclusive \(+\) exhaustive by construction.
  • Rules can then be pruned individually, which may break exclusivity \(\rightarrow\) then class-based ordering is applied.
One model three ways: (a) IF-THEN rules, (b) the decision tree they come from, one rule per root-to-leaf path, (c) a neural network. H&K Fig 1.9.
Sequential covering (direct rule induction) 70 Ch asks CN2 verified/added
  • Learns rules directly from the data, one class at a time.
  • Algorithms: CN2, RIPPER, AQ, FOIL.
  • Steps:
    1. Pick a class. Learn 1 rule that covers many of its tuples and few others.
    2. Remove the tuples that rule covers.
    3. Repeat on what remains until a stopping criterion is met.
  • CN2 specifically: general-to-specific beam search; starts from the empty antecedent and repeatedly appends the test that most improves the rule, scored by entropy and checked by a likelihood-ratio significance test. Produces an ordered rule list (decision list) \(+\) a default rule.

column1: Decision tree classifier vs rule-based classifier
column4:
Decision treeRule-based
Model formOne connected tree; internal node \(=\) attribute test, leaf \(=\) class.An unordered set or an ordered list of IF-THEN rules.
How it is builtDivide and conquer: recursively split the whole data set on the best attribute (Hunt's algorithm, ID3, C4.5, CART).Separate and conquer (sequential covering): learn one rule, remove the tuples it covers, repeat on the remainder (CN2, RIPPER).
CoveragePartitions the space exactly once: rules are automatically mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so every tuple lands in exactly one leaf.Rules may overlap or leave gaps \(\rightarrow\) needs a conflict-resolution strategy (size / class / rule ordering) and a default rule.
Attribute reuseA test near the root constrains every rule below it, so an attribute chosen early is forced on all branches.Each rule is grown independently, so rules need share no condition at all.
PruningPrunes subtrees; removing a node changes every path through it.Prunes individual rules, and may drop conditions from one rule without touching the rest. More flexible, but can break mutual exclusivity.
Replicated subtree problemSuffers from it: the same subtree is duplicated under several branches when the concept is disjunctive.Immune: one rule expresses the disjunct once.
ReadabilityWhole model visible in one diagram; easy to explain end to end, but a deep tree becomes unreadable.Individual rules read very well on their own; a large unordered set is hard to see as a whole.
  • The link worth stating for the marks: a decision tree can always be converted into a rule set by taking one rule per root-to-leaf path, ANDing the conditions along it. The reverse is not true, a general rule set need not correspond to any tree.
  • So the real difference is direct vs indirect induction: rule-based classifiers learn rules straight from the data, decision trees learn a partition and get rules as a by-product.

column1: What is a Nearest Neighbor Classifier? Main issues? Propose a fix.
column4:
Idea
  • Lazy learner / instance-based: stores all training tuples, builds no model.
  • All work happens at query time.
  • “Tell me who your neighbours are and I will tell you who you are.”
Algorithm (KNN)
  1. Choose \(k\) and a distance measure (usually Euclidean).
  2. Compute the distance from the query tuple to every training tuple.
  3. Take the \(k\) smallest \(\rightarrow\) the \(k\) nearest neighbours.
  4. Classification: assign the majority class among those \(k\). Prediction: take their mean value.
  • Normalise the attributes first, else large-range attrs dominate the distance.
  • \(k\) odd for 2 classes \(\rightarrow\) avoids ties.
Choosing \(k\)
  • \(k\) too small \(\rightarrow\) sensitive to noise, overfits.
  • \(k\) too large \(\rightarrow\) neighbourhood includes other classes, underfits.
  • Pick by cross-validation; rule of thumb \(k \approx \sqrt{n}\).
The query \(\times\) with its (a) 1, (b) 2, (c) 3 nearest neighbours: the vote, and so the class, can change with \(k\). Mishra's Ch 3 notes, p13.
Issues (80 Ba asks exactly this)
  • Expensive at query time: \(O(n)\) distance computations per query, no model to shortcut it.
  • Curse of dimensionality: distances lose meaning in high dims.
  • Scale sensitive: needs normalisation.
  • Irrelevant attributes distort distance equally w/ relevant ones.
  • Needs the whole training set in memory.
Fixes / classifier to propose
  • Speed: k-d trees, ball trees, partial distance, editing (drop redundant tuples).
  • Attribute weighting or feature selection for irrelevant attrs.
  • Distance-weighted voting: nearer neighbours count more, \(w = 1/d^2\).
  • Propose an eager learner instead: a decision tree or Naive Bayes builds the model once, then classifies in near-constant time, and ignores irrelevant attrs.

column1: How the distance metric is used in an instance-based classifier
column4:
The four properties, restated §2.4
  1. Non-negativity: \(d(p,q) \ge 0\).
  2. Identity: \(d(p,q) = 0\) iff \(p = q\).
  3. Symmetry: \(d(p,q) = d(q,p)\).
  4. Triangle inequality: \(d(p,r) \le d(p,q) + d(q,r)\).
  • A function with all four is a metric. Euclidean, Manhattan and Minkowski qualify; cosine similarity does not (it is a similarity, not a distance).
Why an instance-based classifier needs each one
  • The classifier is the distance function. KNN stores the tuples and does no other modelling, so every decision it makes is a comparison of distances. A defective metric is a defective classifier.
  • Identity \(\rightarrow\) a training tuple identical to the query is at distance 0, so it is always among the \(k\) nearest. Without it a tuple could fail to match itself.
  • Symmetry \(\rightarrow\) “\(q\) is near \(p\)” and “\(p\) is near \(q\)” agree, so the neighbourhood is well defined however you sort.
  • Triangle inequality \(\rightarrow\) this is the one that pays: it lets k-d trees and ball trees discard an entire branch without measuring the tuples in it, turning an \(O(n)\) scan into roughly \(O(\log n)\). Drop it and every query must compare against the whole training set.
  • Non-negativity \(\rightarrow\) “nearest” means smallest, with a floor at 0.
  • Where the metric enters KNN, step by step: compute \(d\)(query, every training tuple) \(\rightarrow\) sort \(\rightarrow\) take the \(k\) smallest \(\rightarrow\) majority vote (or distance-weighted vote, \(w = 1/d^2\), which uses the actual magnitudes and not just the ordering).
  • Choice of metric changes the answer: Euclidean for continuous attributes, Manhattan when attributes are independent scales, Hamming for nominal attributes, Jaccard for asymmetric binary. Normalise first — an attribute measured in thousands otherwise dominates the sum (§2.4).

column1: Explain Naive Bayesian classification with a suitable example.
column4:
Bayes theorem
\[ P(H|X) = \frac{P(X|H)\,P(H)}{P(X)} \]
  • \(X\) \(=\) the tuple (evidence), \(H\) \(=\) hypothesis “\(X\) belongs to class \(C\)”.
  • \(P(H)\) \(=\) prior: probability of the class before seeing \(X\).
  • \(P(H|X)\) \(=\) posterior: after seeing \(X\). This is what we want.
  • \(P(X|H)\) \(=\) likelihood.  \(P(X)\) \(=\) evidence.
  • 76 Ash asks prior vs posterior directly.
Naive Bayes
  • Classify \(X\) to the class \(C_i\) w/ the largest \(P(C_i|X)\).
  • \(P(X)\) is the same for every class \(\rightarrow\) ignore it; just maximise \(P(X|C_i)P(C_i)\).
  • “Naive” = class-conditional independence assumption: given the class, the attributes are assumed independent, so \[ P(X|C_i) = \prod_{k=1}^{n} P(x_k|C_i) \]
  • That turns 1 hard joint probability into \(n\) easy counts. This is the whole trick.
Algorithm steps (write these, then compute)
  1. Compute the prior \(P(C_i) = |C_{i,D}|/|D|\) for each class.
  2. For each attribute value \(x_k\) in \(X\), compute \(P(x_k|C_i)\) from the counts.
    • Categorical: \(P(x_k|C_i) = |{\rm tuples\ in\ }C_i{\rm\ with\ }x_k| / |C_{i,D}|\).
    • Continuous: assume Gaussian, \(g(x,\mu,\sigma)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\).
  3. Multiply: \(P(X|C_i) = \prod_k P(x_k|C_i)\).
  4. Compute \(P(X|C_i)\,P(C_i)\) for every class.
  5. Predict the class w/ the maximum value.
Laplacian correction 78 Bh short note 4
  • Problem: if any \(P(x_k|C_i)=0\), the whole product collapses to zero, wiping out all the other evidence.
  • Fix: add 1 to every count (and \(k\) to each denominator, \(k\) \(=\) no. of values): \[ P(x_k|C_i) = \frac{n_{k}+1}{|C_{i,D}|+k} \]
  • Eg counts \(0, 990, 10\) \(\rightarrow\) probabilities \(0, 0.990, 0.010\); after correction \(\frac{1}{1003}, \frac{991}{1003}, \frac{11}{1003} = 0.001,\ 0.988,\ 0.011\).
  • Estimates barely move, but the zero is gone.
Bayesian Belief Network (BBN) 3+510
81 Ba, 71 Ch  81 Ba is a numerical \(\rightarrow\) companion.
  • Limitation of Naive Bayes: the independence assumption is almost never true in practice. Correlated attributes get double-counted, which skews the posterior.
  • BBN drops it: allows a subset of attributes to be conditionally dependent.
  • Two parts:
    1. Directed acyclic graph (DAG): node \(=\) variable, arc \(=\) direct causal dependence. Arc \(Y \rightarrow Z\) means \(Y\) is a parent of \(Z\).
    2. Conditional probability table (CPT) at each node, giving \(P(Z\,|\,\text{parents}(Z))\).
  • Joint probability: \(P(x_1,\dots,x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P\big(x_i\,|\,\text{parents}(x_i)\big)\)
  • A node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents.
  • When to use which 71 Ch:
    • Naive Bayes \(\rightarrow\) attributes roughly independent, need speed, little data, many attributes. Eg text/spam classification.
    • BBN \(\rightarrow\) known causal structure and clear dependencies, need to reason w/ missing values. Eg medical diagnosis.
The 81 Ba network and its CPTs. Solved in the companion.
Advantages
  • Fast to train and to classify; single pass over the data.
  • Needs little training data.
  • Handles missing values naturally (skip that factor).
  • Provably optimal when the independence assumption actually holds.
  • Incremental: counts can be updated as data arrives.
Disadvantages
  • Independence assumption rarely holds \(\rightarrow\) accuracy loss on correlated attrs.
  • Zero-frequency problem (needs Laplacian correction).
  • Cannot model interactions between attributes.
  • Continuous attributes need a distribution assumption (usually Gaussian) or discretisation.

column1: How does an ANN classifier work? Explain with algorithm.
column4:
Structure
  • Set of connected units (neurons) in layers, each connection carrying a weight.
  • Input layer (1 unit per attribute) \(\rightarrow\) one or more hidden layers \(\rightarrow\) output layer (1 unit per class).
  • Multilayer feed-forward: no cycles, no connections within a layer.
  • Each unit: net input \(=\sum_i w_i x_i + \theta\) (bias), then an activation function.
  • Sigmoid (logistic): \[ \sigma(\theta) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta}}, \qquad \sigma'(\theta) = \sigma(\theta)\big(1-\sigma(\theta)\big) \]
  • That derivative identity is why sigmoid is used \(\rightarrow\) makes backprop cheap.
The 76 Ch network. Gradients derived in the companion.
Backpropagation algorithm
  1. Initialise weights and biases to small random numbers.
  2. Forward pass: compute net input and output for each unit, layer by layer.
  3. Compute error at the output: \(Err_j = O_j(1-O_j)(T_j - O_j)\) where \(T_j\) \(=\) target.
  4. Backpropagate: for a hidden unit, \(Err_j = O_j(1-O_j)\sum_k Err_k w_{jk}\).
  5. Update weights and biases: \(w_{ij} \mathrel{+}= l\cdot Err_j\cdot O_i\),  \(\theta_j \mathrel{+}= l\cdot Err_j\) (\(l\) \(=\) learning rate).
  6. Repeat until the terminating condition (error small, or epoch limit).
General considerations 72 Ka asks this
  • Network topology: no. of hidden layers and units. Chosen by trial and error; no rule.
  • Input encoding: normalise inputs to \([0,1]\); one unit per nominal value.
  • Output encoding: 1 unit for 2 classes, else 1 per class.
  • Learning rate \(l\): too large \(\rightarrow\) oscillation; too small \(\rightarrow\) slow. Often \(1/t\) w/ epoch \(t\).
  • Initial weights: small random, to break symmetry.
  • Update mode: case updating (per tuple) vs epoch updating (per pass).
Advantages
  • High tolerance of noisy data.
  • Classifies patterns it was not trained on.
  • Works when the relationship is unknown / non-linear.
  • Well suited to continuous-valued inputs and outputs.
  • Inherently parallel.
Disadvantages
  • Black box: poor interpretability, hard to justify a decision.
  • Long training times.
  • Many parameters set empirically (topology, \(l\), epochs).
  • Needs numeric input \(\rightarrow\) encoding effort.
  • Can get stuck in a local minimum.

column1: Confusion matrix: calculate accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall.
column4:
The 4 building blocks
  • TP: positive tuples correctly labelled positive.
  • TN: negative tuples correctly labelled negative.
  • FP: negative tuples wrongly labelled positive (false alarm).
  • FN: positive tuples wrongly labelled negative (miss).
  • \(P = TP+FN\) (all actual positives), \(N = FP+TN\) (all actual negatives).
All the formulas (one table, learn it whole)
MeasureFormula
Accuracy\((TP+TN)/(P+N)\)
Error rate\((FP+FN)/(P+N) = 1-\)accuracy
Sensitivity, recall, TPR\(TP/P\)
Specificity, TNR\(TN/N\)
False alarm rate, FPR\(FP/N = 1-\)specificity
Precision\(TP/(TP+FP)\)
\(F_1\) score\(\dfrac{2\times prec \times rec}{prec+rec}\)
\(F_\beta\)\(\dfrac{(1+\beta^2)\,prec\times rec}{\beta^2 prec+rec}\)
  • Recall \(=\) sensitivity \(=\) TPR. Three names, one thing. Papers use all three.
  • \(F_1\) \(=\) harmonic mean of precision and recall.
THE trap in this chapter. Han & Kamber put actual on the rows, predicted on the columns. The IOE papers flip this between years: 74 Ch and 75 Ash write “Actual \(\backslash\) Predicted”, but 78 Bh and 72 Ch write “Predicted / Actual”.
If you read the orientation wrong, FP and FN swap, so sensitivity and specificity swap and precision is wrong.
Always copy the row/column labels onto your answer sheet first, mark which axis is actual, then compute. verified/added
When accuracy is the wrong measure 80 Ba 3
  • Class imbalance. If 99% of tuples are negative, a classifier that always says “negative” scores 99% accuracy and is useless.
  • Examples: cancer screening, fraud detection, intrusion detection, defect detection.
  • Use instead: sensitivity \(+\) specificity separately, precision/recall, \(F_1\), ROC/AUC, or cost-sensitive measures.
  • Note: \(accuracy = sensitivity\frac{P}{P+N} + specificity\frac{N}{P+N}\) \(\rightarrow\) accuracy hides the split.
Precision vs recall trade-off 74 Ch asks the inverse relation
  • Loosen the threshold \(\rightarrow\) more positives flagged \(\rightarrow\) recall \(\uparrow\), precision \(\downarrow\).
  • Tighten it \(\rightarrow\) precision \(\uparrow\), recall \(\downarrow\).
  • Perfect precision and recall is only possible w/ a perfect classifier \(\rightarrow\) report \(F_1\) to balance them.
ROC curve 73 Shr 1
  • Plot of TPR (y) vs FPR (x) as the decision threshold sweeps.
  • Diagonal \(=\) random guessing. Top-left corner \(=\) perfect.
  • AUC \(=\) area under the curve. Closer to 1 \(=\) better; 0.5 \(=\) useless.
  • Lets you compare 2 classifiers independently of the threshold and of class balance.

column1: Evaluating a classifier: holdout, random subsampling, \(k\)-fold, bootstrap
column4:
MethodWorking mechanismMeritsDemerits
HoldoutPartition \(D\) once at random into a training set and a disjoint test set, typically \(\tfrac{2}{3}\) / \(\tfrac{1}{3}\). Build the model on the first, measure accuracy on the second.Simplest and cheapest: one model is built. Test set is genuinely unseen.Estimate depends entirely on one lucky or unlucky split (high variance). Only part of the data trains, so accuracy is pessimistic on small \(D\).
Random subsamplingHoldout repeated \(k\) times with a fresh random split each time; report the mean of the \(k\) accuracies.Averages the split luck away \(\rightarrow\) much more stable than one holdout. Simple to run.\(k\) models to build. Splits overlap uncontrolled, so some tuples are tested many times and others never, and the runs are not independent.
\(k\)-fold cross-validationSplit \(D\) into \(k\) equal, mutually exclusive folds. In round \(i\) train on all folds but \(D_i\) and test on \(D_i\). Accuracy \(=\) total correct over all \(k\) rounds \(/\;|D|\). \(k=10\) is the recommended value; stratified folds keep each class's proportion.Every tuple is tested exactly once and trains \(k-1\) times \(\rightarrow\) uses the data fully and has low bias and low variance. The standard method, and the safe answer to “which would you use”.Costs \(k\) model builds. Still slightly pessimistic (trains on \(\tfrac{k-1}{k}\) of \(D\)). Leave-one-out (\(k=n\)) removes the bias but is prohibitively expensive and has high variance.
Bootstrap (.632)Sample \(n\) tuples from \(D\) with replacement to form the training set; the tuples never drawn become the test set. A tuple is missed with probability \((1-\tfrac{1}{n})^n \approx e^{-1} = 0.368\), so \(63.2\,\%\) of \(D\) trains on average. Repeat \(b\) times and combine: \(acc = \frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}\big(0.632\,acc_{test_i} + 0.368\,acc_{train_i}\big)\).Best estimator for small data sets, where holdout wastes too much and folds are tiny. Reuses every tuple.Optimistically biased, because duplicated training tuples also reappear in the model. The \(0.632\) weighting is a correction, not a cure. Most expensive of the four.
  • One-line ranking to close the answer: holdout for speed, cross-validation for a trustworthy number, bootstrap when \(D\) is small.
Improving accuracy: ensembles (1 line each is enough)
  • Bagging: train \(k\) models on bootstrap samples, take a majority vote. Reduces variance; helps unstable learners like decision trees.
  • Boosting / AdaBoost: train models sequentially, each re-weighting the tuples the previous one got wrong; weighted vote. Reduces bias; can overfit noise.
  • Random forest: bagging \(+\) a random attribute subset at each split. Robust to overfitting, handles many attributes.

column1: M1. Decision tree by information gain (ID3)
column4:
Method
  1. Compute \(Info(D) = -\sum p_i \log_2 p_i\) for the whole set.
  2. For each attribute \(A\): split \(D\), compute \(Info_A(D)=\sum \frac{|D_j|}{|D|}Info(D_j)\), then \(Gain(A)=Info(D)-Info_A(D)\).
  3. Highest gain wins \(\rightarrow\) becomes the node's test.
  4. Recurse on each branch. Stop when a branch is pure (\(Info = 0\)).
  • Time-savers: a pure partition contributes \(0\); a 50/50 partition contributes exactly \(1\); two partitions with the same class ratio have the same \(Info\), so compute once.
  • \(\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2\). Keep 4 decimals until the end.

  • Split Income as {low, medium} vs {high}:
    • \(D_1\) \(=\) 10 tuples (7 Yes, 3 No): \(Gini = 1-(0.7)^2-(0.3)^2 = 0.420\)
    • \(D_2\) \(=\) 4 tuples (2 Yes, 2 No): \(Gini = 1-(0.5)^2-(0.5)^2 = 0.500\)
    • \(Gini_{Income}(D) = \tfrac{10}{14}(0.420)+\tfrac{4}{14}(0.500) = 0.300+0.143 = 0.443\)
    • \(\Delta Gini = 0.459-0.443 = \mathbf{0.016}\)
  • Split Age as {youth, senior} vs {middle_aged}:
    • \(D_1\) \(=\) 10 tuples (5 Yes, 5 No): \(Gini = 0.500\)
    • \(D_2\) \(=\) 4 tuples (4 Yes, 0 No): \(Gini = \mathbf{0}\) (pure)
    • \(Gini_{Age}(D) = \tfrac{10}{14}(0.500)+\tfrac{4}{14}(0) = 0.357\)
    • \(\Delta Gini = 0.459-0.357 = \mathbf{0.102}\) \(\rightarrow\) best, so Age is chosen
  • Same winner as information gain, which is the usual (not guaranteed) outcome.

Method
  1. Priors: \(P(C_i) = |C_{i,D}|/|D|\).
  2. For each attribute value in \(X\): \(P(x_k|C_i)\) from counts within class \(C_i\).
  3. \(P(X|C_i) = \prod_k P(x_k|C_i)\).
  4. Compare \(P(X|C_i)P(C_i)\) across classes; largest wins.
  • Never divide by \(P(X)\) — it is identical for every class and cancels.
  • Any zero count \(\rightarrow\) apply Laplacian correction \(\frac{n_k+1}{|C_{i,D}|+k}\).
  • Lay the work out as a small table of conditional probabilities; it earns method marks even if arithmetic slips.

Method
  • Sigmoid and its derivative: \(\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\),   \(\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\big(1-\sigma(z)\big)\).
  • Loss \(E=\tfrac{1}{2}(o-t)^2\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial o} = (o-t)\).
  • Apply the chain rule backwards from the loss to the weight in question.

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Chaitra · Q6 · [2+3+4]
Consider the multi-layer feed-forward neural network shown in the following figure. This neural network has three inputs \(x_1\), \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) connected to a hidden layer consisting of two nodes \(h_1\) and \(h_2\). The weight of the edge connecting \(x_i\) to \(h_j\) is \(w_{ji}\). The two hidden nodes are connected to the output node \(o\). The weight of the edge connecting the hidden node \(h_i\) to the output node \(o\) is \(u_i\). The activation functions at hidden and output layers is set to sigmoid function defined as follows: \[ \sigma(\theta) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta}} \] Using the target output \(t\), the squared error is used as the loss function at the output node, and is defined as: \[ E(o,t) = \tfrac{1}{2}(o-t)^2 \]
  1. Using the symbols given above, compute the activation at \(h_1\).
  2. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the output \(o\).
  3. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the weight \(w_{12}\).
column4:
(a) Activation at \(h_1\)
\[ h_1 = \sigma\big(w_{11}x_1 + w_{12}x_2 + w_{13}x_3\big) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(w_{11}x_1+w_{12}x_2+w_{13}x_3)}} \]
(b) Gradient of the loss w.r.t. the output \(o\)
\[ E(o,t)=\tfrac{1}{2}(o-t)^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\partial E}{\partial o} = \mathbf{(o-t)} \]
(c) Gradient of the loss w.r.t. \(w_{12}\)
  • \(w_{12}\) is the weight from \(x_2\) into \(h_1\), so the chain runs \(E \rightarrow o \rightarrow h_1 \rightarrow w_{12}\).
  • Write \(net_o = u_1h_1+u_2h_2\) and \(net_{h_1}=w_{11}x_1+w_{12}x_2+w_{13}x_3\).
\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{12}} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial E}{\partial o}}_{(o-t)}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial o}{\partial net_o}}_{o(1-o)}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial net_o}{\partial h_1}}_{u_1}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial h_1}{\partial net_{h_1}}}_{h_1(1-h_1)}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial net_{h_1}}{\partial w_{12}}}_{x_2} \] \[ \boxed{\ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{12}} = (o-t)\;o(1-o)\;u_1\;h_1(1-h_1)\;x_2\ } \]
  • Sanity checks: the factor \(x_2\) must appear (no input, no gradient); \(u_1\) appears and \(u_2\) does not, because \(w_{12}\) only influences \(o\) through \(h_1\).
  • Weight update: \(w_{12} \leftarrow w_{12} - l\,\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w_{12}}\).
