column1: What is association analysis? Explain its importance in market-basket analysis.
column4:
Definitions
  • Itemset: a set of 1 or more items. \(k\)-itemset \(=\) contains \(k\) items.
  • Transaction \(T\): a set of items bought together. \(D\) \(=\) the whole database.
  • Association rule: an implication \(A \Rightarrow B\) where \(A \subset I\), \(B \subset I\), and \(A \cap B = \emptyset\).
  • Association analysis: finding all rules that satisfy a minimum support and a minimum confidence.
The 2 measures (learn both definitions exactly)
\(\sigma(X)\) \(=\) support count of \(X\) (how many transactions contain it), \(|D|\) \(=\) total transactions. \[ sup(A \Rightarrow B) = P(A \cup B) = \frac{\sigma(A \cup B)}{|D|} \] \[ conf(A \Rightarrow B) = P(B|A) = \frac{\sigma(A \cup B)}{\sigma(A)} \]
  • Support \(\rightarrow\) how frequent. Filters out rules with too little evidence.
  • Confidence \(\rightarrow\) how reliable. Strength of the implication.
  • A rule is strong if it meets both thresholds.
  • Support is symmetric (\(A\cup B\)), confidence is not (\(A\Rightarrow B \ne B\Rightarrow A\)).
Market basket analysis 75 Ch short note
  • Analyses which items customers put in the basket together.
  • Classic result: {nappies} => {beer}.
  • Uses: shelf layout, cross-selling, product bundling, catalogue design, promotion planning, recommendation (“customers who bought this also bought…”).
  • Actionable both ways: put them together to increase convenience, or far apart to force the customer past other shelves.
2-step process (every algorithm does this)
  1. Find all frequent itemsets: those with support \(\ge\) min_sup. This is the expensive step and is what Apriori / FP-Growth optimise.
  2. Generate strong rules from them: for each frequent itemset \(l\), take every non-empty proper subset \(s\) and output \(s \Rightarrow (l-s)\) if \(\frac{sup\_count(l)}{sup\_count(s)} \ge\) min_conf.
  3. A \(k\)-itemset yields \(2^k - 2\) candidate rules.
Applications beyond retail 80 Ba asks where it is applicable
  • Web usage / click-stream mining, medical symptom-disease co-occurrence, gene co-occurrence (Ch 1), fraud detection, intrusion detection, text mining.

column1: Pattern evaluation: why support–confidence is not enough
column4:
The problem
  • A rule can clear both thresholds and still be completely misleading.
  • Classic case: 10,000 txns, 6,000 contain game, 7,500 contain video, 4,000 contain both.
    • \(support = 4000/10000 = \mathbf{40\%}\) (passes)
    • \(confidence(game \Rightarrow video) = 4000/6000 = \mathbf{66\%}\) (passes)
    • But \(P(video) = \mathbf{75\%}\) on its own, higher than 66%.
    • Buying a game makes you less likely to buy a video. The “strong” rule is negatively correlated.
  • Cause: confidence ignores the support of the consequent.
Correlation measures verified/added
\[ lift(A,B) = \frac{P(A\cup B)}{P(A)P(B)} = \frac{conf(A\Rightarrow B)}{sup(B)} \]
  • \(>1\) positively correlated \(\cdot\) \(<1\) negative \(\cdot\) \(=1\) independent.
  • Above: \(lift = 0.40/(0.60\times0.75) = \mathbf{0.89} < 1\) \(\rightarrow\) caught.
\[ \chi^2 = \sum \frac{(observed-expected)^2}{expected} \]
  • Above: \(\chi^2 = 555.6\), and observed \(<\) expected \(\rightarrow\) negative correlation.
4 null-invariant measures
  • \(all\_conf(A,B) = \dfrac{sup(A\cup B)}{\max\{sup(A),sup(B)\}} = \min\{P(A|B),P(B|A)\}\)
  • \(max\_conf(A,B) = \max\{P(A|B),P(B|A)\}\)
  • \(Kulc(A,B) = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(P(A|B)+P(B|A)\big)\)
  • \(cosine(A,B) = \dfrac{sup(A\cup B)}{\sqrt{sup(A)\times sup(B)}}\)
  • Null-invariant \(=\) unaffected by the number of transactions containing neither item. lift and \(\chi^2\) are NOT null-invariant, so they distort on sparse data.
  • Use Kulc \(+\) imbalance ratio together for the clearest reading.

column1: Why a 100 % confidence rule is uninteresting, and why 99 % is
column4:
100 %: true by construction, so it teaches nothing
  • \(conf(A \Rightarrow B) = 100\,\%\) means every transaction holding \(A\) also holds \(B\), no exceptions anywhere in \(D\).
  • Almost always that is a property of the schema, not of the customers \(\rightarrow\) already known before mining started:
    • Definitional: {pregnant} => {female}, {Corolla} => {car}.
    • Taxonomic: {Kathmandu} => {Nepal}, item \(\rightarrow\) its own category.
    • Subset artefact: {milk, bread} => {milk}. Consequent already sits inside the antecedent's itemset.
    • Bundled by a business rule: free gift always shipped with the product, so the pair can never come apart.
  • No headroom, so no action. You cannot lift sales of \(B\) by promoting \(A\): everyone who takes \(A\) takes \(B\) already. Cross-selling, shelf layout and recommendation all have nothing to work with.
  • Such rules are also generated in bulk (every frequent itemset spawns its own subset rules) and bury the genuine findings. Fix: a maximum support threshold, or drop rules whose consequent is implied by the antecedent.
99 %: real regularity, and the 1 % is the payload
  • A definitional rule cannot have exceptions. So 99 % proves the dependency is empirical, discovered from behaviour rather than built into the data dictionary.
  • It is still near-deterministic \(\rightarrow\) strong enough to predict on, unlike a 60 % rule.
  • The interest is in the 1 % that breaks it, and it reads two ways. Give both:
    1. The exceptions are wrong \(\rightarrow\) candidate data-quality defects: mis-keyed records, typos, a faulty sensor, a duplicated ID. Near-100 % rules are used exactly this way to discover integrity constraints and clean a warehouse (Ch 2).
    2. The exceptions are real \(\rightarrow\) candidate anomalies: fraud, intrusion, a defective batch, a customer segment behaving unlike every other. This is the association-rule route into anomaly detection (Ch 6).
  • Practical value too: 1 % is small but non-empty, so the customers who take \(A\) without \(B\) are a precisely targetable list.
  • One line worth memorising: a 100 % rule tells you about the schema, a 99 % rule tells you about the world, and its exceptions are where the interesting cases live.

column1: Explain the Apriori algorithm / principle with example.
column4:
The Apriori property (state this, it is the answer)
  • All non-empty subsets of a frequent itemset must also be frequent.
  • Contrapositive, and the one actually used: if an itemset is infrequent, all of its supersets are infrequent \(\rightarrow\) prune them without counting.
  • This is anti-monotonicity: support never increases as an itemset grows.
  • Effect: turns a \(2^n\) brute-force search into something tractable. 71 Ch asks exactly this, 10.
Brute force, for contrast
  • \(n\) items \(\rightarrow\) \(2^n-1\) candidate itemsets, each needing a database scan.
  • Apriori prunes the lattice level by level instead.
Algorithm
  1. Scan \(D\), count each item \(\rightarrow\) keep those \(\ge\) min_sup \(\rightarrow\) \(L_1\).
  2. Repeat for \(k = 2,3,\dots\) until \(L_{k-1}\) is empty:
    1. Join: \(C_k = L_{k-1} \bowtie L_{k-1}\). Join 2 itemsets only if their first \(k-2\) items are identical (keeps items sorted, avoids duplicates).
    2. Prune: drop any candidate having any \((k-1)\)-subset not in \(L_{k-1}\).
    3. Count: scan \(D\) once, count the survivors.
    4. \(L_k\) \(=\) candidates meeting min_sup.
  3. Answer \(=\bigcup_k L_k\).
Then generate rules
  • For each frequent \(l\), for each non-empty proper subset \(s\): output \(s\Rightarrow(l-s)\) if \(\frac{sup(l)}{sup(s)} \ge\) min_conf.
  • When no rule can exist at any confidence 79 Ba 3 verified/added: a rule needs a proper non-empty subset, so it needs a frequent itemset of size \(\ge 2\). If \(L_2 = \emptyset\) (every frequent itemset is a single item), then no rule exists for any confidence threshold, including 0 % \(\rightarrow\) lowering min_conf cannot help, only lowering min_sup can. Check \(L_2\) before answering, never the confidence value.
Advantages
  • Simple, easy to implement and to explain.
  • Uses a level-wise search that is easy to parallelise.
  • The pruning is provably safe (no frequent itemset is ever lost).
Disadvantages (the setup for FP-Growth)
  • Generates a huge number of candidates. \(10^4\) frequent 1-itemsets \(\rightarrow\) about \(10^7\) candidate 2-itemsets.
  • Requires repeated database scans — one per level, so \(k+1\) scans for a \(k\)-itemset. Very costly on disk-resident data.
  • Struggles with long patterns and with low min_sup.
The level-wise run, drawn
  • H&K's 9-transaction example, min count 2: \(C_1 \rightarrow L_1\), join to \(C_2\), scan, \(L_2\), join and prune to \(C_3\), scan, \(L_3\).
  • Only 2 candidates survive into \(C_3\): every other 3-itemset has an infrequent 2-subset, so it is dropped without a scan. That is the Apriori property at work.
  • This is the shape every numerical in the companion writes out. H&K Fig 6.2.

column1: What is FP-Growth? Explain with example. How does it overcome Apriori's problems?
column4:
Key idea
  • Generate NO candidates at all.
  • Compress \(D\) into a frequent-pattern tree (FP-tree), then mine that tree by divide and conquer.
  • Only 2 database scans in total, against Apriori's \(k+1\).
Step 1: build the FP-tree
  1. Scan 1: count every item. Discard the infrequent ones.
  2. Sort the frequent items by descending support \(\rightarrow\) the F-list. Break ties consistently (alphabetically) and say so.
  3. Scan 2: for each transaction, keep only frequent items, reorder them into F-list order, and insert that path into the tree.
    • Share a prefix with an existing path \(\rightarrow\) just increment those counts.
    • Otherwise create new nodes with count 1.
  4. Maintain a header table: one entry per frequent item, with a node-link chain threading every occurrence of that item in the tree.
  • Why descending order: the most common items sit near the root, so paths share prefixes and the tree stays small.
Step 2: mine the tree (FP-Growth)
  1. Work bottom-up through the header table, ie least frequent item first.
  2. For item \(\alpha\), follow its node-links to collect its conditional pattern base \(=\) every prefix path leading to \(\alpha\), each carrying \(\alpha\)'s count at that node.
  3. Build the conditional FP-tree from that base, keeping only items that are still frequent within it.
  4. Recurse on the conditional tree, concatenating \(\alpha\) to each pattern found.
  5. If a conditional tree is a single path, just enumerate all subsets of that path.
A finished FP-tree: null root, item:count nodes, and the header table (item, support) whose dashed node-links thread every occurrence of an item. Step 2 walks those links. H&K Fig 6.7.

column1: How do you handle categorical attributes in data mining? Issues and fixes.
column4:
The problem
  • Association analysis assumes asymmetric binary items (present / absent).
  • Real tables hold categorical (Gender, Region) and continuous (Age, Income) attributes.
Handling: binarisation
  • Convert each (attribute, value) pair into one binary item.
  • Eg Gender \(\rightarrow\) items Gender=Male, Gender=Female.
  • Continuous attributes must be discretised first \(\rightarrow\) Ch 2, §2.2, then binarised.
Issues that arise (this is what 73 Shr wants)
  • Too many items: an attribute with many values explodes the item count. Fix: group rare values into an “Other” category.
  • Many items are infrequent: rare values never reach min_sup, so patterns involving them are lost. Fix: lower min_sup, or use a per-item threshold.
  • Some items are far too frequent: eg Gender=Male at \(\approx\)50% produces masses of trivial redundant rules. Fix: set a maximum support threshold too.
  • Redundancy: values of one attribute are mutually exclusive, so an itemset containing Gender=Male and Gender=Female has support 0 by construction. Fix: never generate candidates that pair 2 values of the same attribute.
  • Loss of ordering for ordinal attributes after binarisation.
column5: PIN 3 79 Bh, 73 Shr, 72 Ch
column9: ch4 theory tier::PIN yr::72-Ch yr::73-Shr yr::79-Bh

column4:
Sequential patterns
  • A sequence is an ordered list of elements; each element is an unordered set of items. \(s = \langle e_1 e_2 \dots e_n\rangle\).
  • Length \(=\) number of items; a \(k\)-sequence has \(k\) items. Not the number of elements — this is the usual mistake.
  • Subsequence: \(\langle a_1 \dots a_m\rangle\) is a subsequence of \(\langle b_1 \dots b_n\rangle\) if there exist \(i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_m\) with \(a_1 \subseteq b_{i_1},\ \dots,\ a_m \subseteq b_{i_m}\).
    • Order across elements must be preserved; within an element it need not be.
  • Support of a sequence \(=\) fraction of data sequences containing it.
  • Algorithms: AprioriAll 76 Ash short note, GSP, SPADE, PrefixSpan. AprioriAll applies the same anti-monotone pruning to sequences.
  • Uses: web click-streams, purchase sequences over time, DNA, telephone call patterns.
Subgraph patterns 79 Bh 2
  • Data \(=\) a collection of graphs (molecules, web fragments, social networks).
  • A frequent subgraph is one appearing in at least min_sup of them.
  • Candidate generation by growing, 2 schemes:
    • Vertex growing: join 2 graphs sharing a common subgraph, add 1 vertex.
    • Edge growing: join 2 graphs sharing a core, add 1 edge. Preferred — it generates fewer candidates.
  • The hard part is graph isomorphism: deciding whether 2 drawings are the same graph. Handled with a canonical labelling.
  • Algorithms: AGM, FSG, gSpan.
Infrequent / negative patterns
  • A negative pattern is a set of items that appear together far less often than independence would predict.
  • Eg {Coke, Pepsi} — customers buy one or the other.
  • Useful for detecting substitute products and for fraud (a combination that should never occur).
  • Hard because support is anti-monotone, so “infrequent” cannot be pruned the same way.
Subgraph terms, drawn
(a) a labelled graph; (b) a subgraph: some of its vertices and edges; (c) an induced subgraph: some vertices and every edge between them. Candidate generation grows these one vertex or one edge at a time. Mishra's Ch 4 notes, p9.

column4:
5 methods \(\cdot\) 14 PYQ instances \(\cdot\) every itemset count recomputed from the printed transaction tables. This is the heaviest numerical chapter in the syllabus.
Methods
  • M1 Apriori: candidate generation, pruning, frequent itemsets
  • M2 Rule generation from frequent itemsets
  • M3 FP-tree construction and FP-Growth mining
  • M4 Pattern evaluation: lift and the correlation measures
  • M5 Subsequence enumeration
Convert the threshold to a COUNT before you start. “min support 50%” on 6 transactions means a count of 3. Nearly every lost mark in this chapter comes from mixing percentages and counts half way through. Write min_sup_count \(=\) N at the top and use only that.
Also: support is over ALL transactions; confidence is over the antecedent's transactions only.

Method
  1. Scan once, count items \(\rightarrow\) keep those \(\ge\) min_sup_count \(\rightarrow\) \(L_1\).
  2. Join \(L_{k-1}\) with itself: combine 2 itemsets only if their first \(k-2\) items match.
  3. Prune: discard a candidate if any of its \((k-1)\)-subsets is missing from \(L_{k-1}\).
  4. Count survivors against \(D\), keep those meeting the threshold \(\rightarrow\) \(L_k\).
  5. Stop when \(L_k\) is empty.
  • Show the prune step explicitly — it is where the method marks are.

column1: M2. Rule generation from frequent itemsets
column4:
Method
  • For each frequent itemset \(l\) with \(|l| \ge 2\), take every non-empty proper subset \(s\): \[ s \Rightarrow (l-s) \quad\text{with}\quad conf = \frac{sup\_count(l)}{sup\_count(s)} \]
  • Keep it if \(conf \ge\) min_conf. A \(k\)-itemset gives \(2^k-2\) candidate rules.
  • The support of every rule from \(l\) is the same (\(= sup(l)\)); only confidence varies.
  • Shortcut: if \(s \Rightarrow (l-s)\) fails, every rule whose antecedent is a subset of \(s\) also fails. Prune downward.

column4:
Method
\[ lift(A,B) = \frac{P(A\cup B)}{P(A)\,P(B)} = \frac{conf(A\Rightarrow B)}{sup(B)} \qquad \chi^2 = \sum\frac{(obs-exp)^2}{exp} \]

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2070 Chaitra · Q5 · [8]
Why is pattern evaluation important in association rule mining? Explain with example the statistical based measures used for measuring interestingness of association rules.
column4:
The paper prints no data — the example is yours to supply. The standard game / video contingency table below is the one every textbook uses. verified/added
Given
10,000 transactions: 6,000 contain game, 7,500 contain video, 4,000 contain both.
Step 1: the support–confidence view says the rule is strong
  • \(sup(game \Rightarrow video) = 4000/10000 = \mathbf{40\%}\) (passes a 30% threshold)
  • \(conf(game \Rightarrow video) = 4000/6000 = \mathbf{66.7\%}\) (passes a 60% threshold)
Step 2: but look at the consequent alone
  • \(P(video) = 7500/10000 = \mathbf{75\%}\)
  • Buying a game DROPS the chance of buying a video from 75% to 66.7%. The rule is actively misleading.
Step 3: lift catches it
\[ lift = \frac{0.40}{0.60 \times 0.75} = \frac{0.40}{0.45} = \mathbf{0.89} < 1 \ \rightarrow\ \text{negatively correlated} \]
Step 4: \(\chi^2\) agrees
game\(\overline{game}\)row

\(\overline{video}\)2000 (1500)500 (1000)2500

\[ \chi^2 = \tfrac{500^2}{4500}+\tfrac{500^2}{3000}+\tfrac{500^2}{1500}+\tfrac{500^2}{1000} = 55.6+83.3+166.7+250 = \mathbf{555.6} \]
  • Large \(\chi^2\) \(\rightarrow\) correlated; observed (4000) \(<\) expected (4500) \(\rightarrow\) negatively.
Final answer
  • Pattern evaluation matters because support and confidence alone certify rules that are false. Add a correlation measure before reporting any rule.

Method
  • A \(k\)-subsequence contains \(k\) items in total (not \(k\) elements).
  • Choose how many items to take from each element, keeping element order; a chosen element must be non-empty to remain in the sequence.
  • Enumerate systematically by the split \((a,b,c,d)\) of items taken per element, then remove duplicates.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Chaitra · Q8 (a) · [3]
List all the 4-subsequences contained in the data sequence: \(\langle \{1,3\}\ \{2\}\ \{2,3\}\ \{4\} \rangle\)
column4:
Given
\(e_1=\{1,3\}\), \(e_2=\{2\}\), \(e_3=\{2,3\}\), \(e_4=\{4\}\); 6 items in total.
What counts as a subsequence (get this right first)
  • Take a subset from each element, possibly empty. Elements chosen empty simply disappear.
  • Element order must be preserved, and items from two different elements can never be merged into one element.
  • A \(k\)-subsequence has \(k\) items in total, counted across all surviving elements. It is not \(k\) elements. This is the single most common misreading.
  • So \(\langle\{1,3\}\{2\}\rangle\) is a 3-subsequence, not a 2-subsequence.
Why enumerate by splits
  • A choice is fully described by how many items are taken from each element, written \((a,b,c,d)\) for \(e_1 \ldots e_4\).
  • The bounds are the element sizes: \(a\le2\), \(b\le1\), \(c\le2\), \(d\le1\), and we need \(a+b+c+d = 4\).
  • For a fixed split the number of ways is a product of binomials, \(\binom{2}{a}\binom{1}{b}\binom{2}{c}\binom{1}{d}\), because the elements are chosen independently.
  • Enumerating splits first guarantees nothing is missed, which listing by hand does not. Then remove duplicates at the end.
Step 1: enumerate the item-count splits
\((a,b,c,d)\) with \(a\le2, b\le1, c\le2, d\le1\), sum \(=4\)
\((a,b,c,d)\)WaysSubsequences
(2,1,1,0)2\(\langle\{1,3\}\{2\}\{2\}\rangle\), \(\langle\{1,3\}\{2\}\{3\}\rangle\)
(2,1,0,1)1\(\langle\{1,3\}\{2\}\{4\}\rangle\)
(2,0,2,0)1\(\langle\{1,3\}\{2,3\}\rangle\)
(2,0,1,1)2\(\langle\{1,3\}\{2\}\{4\}\rangle\) (duplicate), \(\langle\{1,3\}\{3\}\{4\}\rangle\)
(1,1,2,0)2\(\langle\{1\}\{2\}\{2,3\}\rangle\), \(\langle\{3\}\{2\}\{2,3\}\rangle\)
(1,1,1,1)4\(\langle\{1\}\{2\}\{2\}\{4\}\rangle\), \(\langle\{1\}\{2\}\{3\}\{4\}\rangle\), \(\langle\{3\}\{2\}\{2\}\{4\}\rangle\), \(\langle\{3\}\{2\}\{3\}\{4\}\rangle\)
(1,0,2,1)2\(\langle\{1\}\{2,3\}\{4\}\rangle\), \(\langle\{3\}\{2,3\}\{4\}\rangle\)
(0,1,2,1)1\(\langle\{2\}\{2,3\}\{4\}\rangle\)
Step 2: check the count, then remove duplicates
  • Ways per split: \(2+1+1+2+2+4+2+1 = \mathbf{15}\) selections. Do this arithmetic — it is how you know no split was dropped.
  • A duplicate appears when the same items can be taken from different elements. Here \(e_2 = \{2\}\) and \(e_3 = \{2,3\}\) share the item 2, so \(\langle\{1,3\}\{2\}\{4\}\rangle\) is produced twice: once as \((2,1,0,1)\) taking the 2 from \(e_2\), once as \((2,0,1,1)\) taking it from \(e_3\). Same sequence, so it counts once.
  • No other pair of splits can collide, because every other split keeps a different number of surviving elements or a different element content.
Final answer
  • 15 selections \(-\) 1 duplicate \(\rightarrow\) 14 distinct 4-subsequences.
  • The exam usually only wants “at least four” 79 Bh, so listing the first few from a clearly stated method is enough. Show the method, not just the list.

column1: M6. Subgraph candidate generation by edge growing
column4:
Method
  • Two frequent subgraphs are joined only if they share a common core: the subgraph left when one edge is removed from each.
  • Edge growing joins two \(k\)-edge graphs sharing a \((k-1)\)-edge core and produces a \((k+1)\)-edge candidate \(=\) core \(+\) the edge unique to each parent.
  • Vertex growing instead adds a vertex, and generates far more candidates. Edge growing is preferred for exactly that reason.
  • The trap, and the whole point of this question: when the core carries repeated vertex labels, the two extra edges can be attached in more than one non-isomorphic way, so one join yields several candidates. Enumerate them, do not assume there is one.
column7: M6. Subgraph candidate generation by edge growing

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Chaitra · Q8 (b) · [3]
Draw all candidate sub-graphs obtained from joining the pair of graphs shown below using edge-growing method to expand the sub-graphs.
column4:
Step 1: read the two parents
  • Both are a 4-cycle of \(a\) vertices with two pendant vertices hanging off two adjacent corners of that cycle.
  • \(G_1\): pendants are \(b\) and \(b\).  \(G_2\): pendants are \(b\) and \(c\).
  • Each has 6 vertices and 6 edges, so \(k = 6\).
Step 2: find the core
  • Delete one edge from each so that what is left is the same graph: drop the second pendant edge from both.
  • Core \(=\) 4-cycle of \(a\)'s \(+\) one pendant \(b\), 5 vertices and 5 edges \(= k-1\). ✓ the graphs are joinable.
  • Edge unique to \(G_1\): \(a - b\).  Edge unique to \(G_2\): \(a - c\).
Step 3: the candidate size
  • Candidate \(=\) core \(+\) both unique edges \(\rightarrow\) \(5 + 2 = \mathbf{7}\) edges, 7 vertices.
Step 4: where can the two new edges attach?
  • Call the core's pendant-carrying \(a\) vertex \(A_1\). In both parents the second pendant sits on a cycle vertex adjacent to \(A_1\), and \(A_1\) has two neighbours in the cycle, \(A_2\) and \(A_4\).
  • All four placements \((b,c)\) are legal: \((A_2,A_2)\), \((A_4,A_4)\), \((A_2,A_4)\), \((A_4,A_2)\).
  • The core has a mirror symmetry swapping \(A_2\) and \(A_4\), so these collapse to two non-isomorphic candidates:
    • \((A_2,A_2)\cong(A_4,A_4)\) \(\rightarrow\) candidate I
    • \((A_2,A_4)\cong(A_4,A_2)\) \(\rightarrow\) candidate II
  • This multiplicity comes entirely from the four \(a\)'s sharing one label. Had the cycle been \(a,b,c,d\) the join would have given a single candidate.
Final answer: 2 candidate sub-graphs, each with 7 vertices and 7 edges

column1: What is cluster analysis? Applications? How does it differ from classification?
column4:
Definition
  • Cluster \(=\) a collection of objects similar within the group and dissimilar to objects in other groups.
  • Cluster analysis \(=\) grouping objects so that intra-cluster similarity is maximised and inter-cluster similarity minimised.
  • Unsupervised: no class labels are given. The classes are the output, not the input.
  • Also called unsupervised classification or segmentation.
Clustering vs classification 72 Ka 5
ClassificationClustering
LearningSupervisedUnsupervised
LabelsGiven in trainingNone; discovered
GoalPredict a known labelFind the groups themselves
EvaluationAccuracy vs truthCohesion / separation
ClassesFixed, knownNumber often unknown
Applications asked in 5 papers
  • Market segmentation: group customers by behaviour.
  • Document / search-result grouping, topic discovery.
  • Image segmentation and pattern recognition.
  • Biology: taxonomy of species, gene expression grouping.
  • Land use from satellite data; city planning; earthquake epicentre grouping.
  • Outlier detection — points in no cluster \(\rightarrow\) Ch 6.
  • Data reduction / preprocessing step for other algorithms.
Requirements of a good clustering method
  • Scalability; handles mixed attribute types; finds arbitrary shapes.
  • Minimal domain knowledge for parameters; copes with noise and outliers.
  • Insensitive to input order; handles high dimensionality; interpretable and usable.
Types of clusters (81 Ba asks this directly)
  • Well-separated: every point is closer to all points in its own cluster than to any point outside. The ideal case.
  • Prototype-based (centre-based): each point is closer to its cluster's centroid (mean) or medoid (most central actual point) than to any other. \(\rightarrow\) what K-means finds.
  • Contiguity-based (nearest neighbour) 71 Shr 10: each point is closer to at least one point in its cluster than to any point outside. Handles chains and irregular shapes; breaks down when noise bridges 2 clusters. \(\rightarrow\) single-link hierarchical, or DBSCAN.
Prototype-based, found by K-means iterating (§5.2)
(a) initial clustering around the seeds; (b) centroids recomputed and points reassigned; (c) final, once the assignment stops changing. H&K Fig 10.3.
  • Density-based: a cluster is a dense region separated by low-density regions. Handles arbitrary shapes and noise. \(\rightarrow\) DBSCAN.
  • Conceptual (shared-property): points share some general property, not just proximity. Needs a concept definition.
Types of clustering methods
  • Partitioning: K-means, K-medoids/PAM, CLARA.
  • Hierarchical: AGNES, DIANA, BIRCH, Chameleon.
  • Density-based: DBSCAN, OPTICS, DENCLUE.
  • Grid-based: STING, CLIQUE, WaveCluster.
  • Model-based: EM, COBWEB, SOM.
Grid-based, in 3 steps NEW
  • Partition the data space into a multi-dim grid of finite cells.
  • Compute cell statistics: count, mean, density per cell.
  • Merge adjacent cells above a density threshold into clusters.
  • Why it is the fast one: cost depends on the number of cells, not the number of points \(\rightarrow\) scales to huge datasets. Price paid: resolution is capped by cell size.

column1: Write the K-means algorithm. Explain with example and state its limitations.
column4:
Algorithm (write these 5 steps, then compute)
  1. Choose \(K\), the number of clusters.
  2. Initialise \(K\) centroids (usually \(K\) randomly chosen data points).
  3. Assign each point to the cluster whose centroid is nearest (Euclidean).
  4. Recompute each centroid as the mean of the points assigned to it.
  5. Repeat 3–4 until the assignment stops changing (or centroids move less than a tolerance, or a max iteration count is hit).
Objective function
\[ SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{x \in C_i} dist(x, c_i)^2 \]
  • K-means minimises SSE (within-cluster sum of squared error).
  • The mean is provably the point minimising SSE for a cluster — that is why step 4 uses the mean.
  • Complexity \(O(nKId)\): \(n\) points, \(K\) clusters, \(I\) iterations, \(d\) dimensions. Linear in \(n\) \(\rightarrow\) scales well.
Choosing \(K\) 80 Ba 4
  • Elbow method: plot SSE against \(K\); take the \(K\) where the curve bends. SSE always falls as \(K\) rises, so the bend, not the minimum, is the answer.
  • Silhouette coefficient: pick the \(K\) maximising it.
  • Domain knowledge; cross-validation; gap statistic.
  • Rule of thumb \(K \approx \sqrt{n/2}\).
Limitations (asked with almost every numerical)
  • \(K\) must be given in advance.
  • Sensitive to the initial centroids \(\rightarrow\) different seeds give different clusterings; converges to a local optimum, not the global one. Fix: run several times and keep the lowest SSE, or use K-means++.
  • Sensitive to outliers: the mean is dragged by extreme values. Fix: K-medoids.
  • Only finds convex, roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters. Fails on elongated or nested shapes.
  • Cannot handle categorical data (no mean). Fix: K-modes.
  • Empty clusters can occur; needs a re-seeding rule.
K-medoids (PAM)
  • Uses an actual data point (the medoid) as the cluster centre instead of the mean.
  • Minimises the sum of absolute distances rather than squared distances.
  • Far more robust to outliers and works with any distance measure.
  • Cost: \(O(K(n-K)^2)\) per iteration \(\rightarrow\) much slower; CLARA samples to scale it.
Bisecting K-means 71 Ch 10
  • Hybrid: produces a hierarchy using K-means as the engine.
  • Steps:
    1. Start with all points in one cluster.
    2. Pick a cluster to split (largest, or highest SSE).
    3. Split it in two with K-means (\(K=2\)); do this several times and keep the best split.
    4. Repeat until \(K\) clusters exist.
  • Less sensitive to initialisation than plain K-means, and gives a dendrogram.

    2. Pick a cluster to split (largest, or highest SSE).
    3. Split it in two with K-means (\(K=2\)); do this several times and keep the best split.
    4. Repeat until \(K\) clusters exist.
  • Less sensitive to initialisation than plain K-means, and gives a dendrogram.

column1: What is hierarchical clustering? Agglomerative vs divisive. Draw the dendrogram.
column4:
Idea
  • Produces a nested tree of clusters, not a single flat partition.
  • No need to specify \(K\) in advance — cut the dendrogram at any height to get any \(K\).
  • Dendrogram: tree diagram where the height of a merge \(=\) the distance between the two clusters merged.
Two directions
  • Agglomerative (AGNES) — bottom-up, the common one.
    1. Start: every point is its own cluster.
    2. Merge the two closest clusters.
    3. Update the distance matrix.
    4. Repeat until one cluster remains.
  • Divisive (DIANA) — top-down.
    1. Start: all points in one cluster.
    2. Split the cluster that is least cohesive.
    3. Repeat until every point is alone (or a stopping rule fires).
  • Divisive is more expensive (\(2^{n-1}-1\) ways to split), so agglomerative dominates.
AGNES merges \(a..e\) upward in steps 0 to 4; DIANA splits them downward in the reverse order. H&K Fig 10.6.
Linkage: how to measure cluster-to-cluster distance (this is the whole exam question)
  • Single link (MIN): distance \(=\) closest pair between the 2 clusters.
    • \(+\) Finds arbitrary, elongated shapes.
    • \(-\) Chaining effect: a line of noise points can bridge 2 real clusters.
  • Complete link (MAX): distance \(=\) farthest pair.
    • \(+\) Less sensitive to noise, gives compact balanced clusters.
    • \(-\) Biased to globular shapes; breaks large clusters.
  • Average link: mean of all pairwise distances. A compromise.
  • Centroid / Ward's: distance between centroids / merge that increases SSE least.
Pros and cons
  • \(+\) No \(K\) needed; the dendrogram is highly interpretable; any \(K\) obtainable afterwards.
  • \(-\) \(O(n^2)\) space and \(O(n^3)\) time \(\rightarrow\) does not scale.
  • \(-\) Merges are irreversible — a bad merge can never be undone (greedy).
The same merges as a dendrogram, level \(l=0\) (all apart) to \(l=4\) (one cluster); cut at any level for that many clusters. H&K Fig 10.7.

column1: What are core, border and noise points? Write the DBSCAN algorithm and how it handles noise.
column4:
Two parameters
  • \(\varepsilon\) (Eps) \(=\) the neighbourhood radius.
  • MinPts \(=\) minimum number of points required inside that radius.
  • \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood: \(N_\varepsilon(p) = \{q \in D \mid dist(p,q) \le \varepsilon\}\)
Three kinds of point (learn these exactly)
  • Core point: \(|N_\varepsilon(p)| \ge\) MinPts. Sits in the interior of a cluster.
  • Border point: fewer than MinPts neighbours, but lies within \(\varepsilon\) of a core point. On the edge.
  • Noise point: neither. Discarded — this is how DBSCAN handles noise.
The reachability definitions 74 Ash short note
  • Directly density-reachable: \(q\) is directly density-reachable from \(p\) if \(p\) is a core point and \(q \in N_\varepsilon(p)\).
  • Density-reachable: there is a chain \(p_1,\dots,p_n\) where each \(p_{i+1}\) is directly density-reachable from \(p_i\). Not symmetric (the end may be a border point).
  • Density-connected: \(p\) and \(q\) are density-connected if some object \(o\) exists from which both are density-reachable. This one IS symmetric.
  • A cluster \(=\) a maximal set of density-connected points.
Circles are \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhoods, MinPts \(=3\). Left: \(m, p\) are core, \(q\) is density-reachable from \(p\) through \(m\), but not the reverse (\(q\) is a border point). Right: \(r\) and \(s\) are density-connected through \(o\). H&K Fig 10.14.
Algorithm
  1. Label every point as core, border or noise by counting its \(\varepsilon\)-neighbours.
  2. Discard the noise points.
  3. Put an edge between every pair of core points within \(\varepsilon\) of each other.
  4. Each connected group of core points becomes a cluster.
  5. Assign each border point to a cluster of one of its associated core points.
Choosing the parameters 78 Bh asks this
  • \(k\)-distance plot: for each point compute the distance to its \(k\)th nearest neighbour (\(k =\) MinPts), sort descending, plot. The sharp bend (knee) gives \(\varepsilon\).
  • Rule of thumb: MinPts \(\ge d+1\), commonly \(2\times d\) for \(d\) dimensions; MinPts \(=4\) for 2-D.
Pros
  • Finds arbitrarily shaped clusters.  \(\bullet\) \(K\) is not needed.
  • Explicitly identifies noise / outliers rather than forcing every point into a cluster.
  • Insensitive to the order of points (except some border cases).
Cons and their fixes 76 Ash asks “how do we avoid the issues”
  • Fails on clusters of varying density — one \((\varepsilon,\text{MinPts})\) pair cannot suit both a dense and a sparse cluster. Fix: OPTICS, which orders points across a range of \(\varepsilon\).
  • Very sensitive to the 2 parameters. Fix: the \(k\)-distance plot.
  • Degrades in high dimensions (distance loses meaning). Fix: reduce dimensions first.
  • A border point reachable from 2 clusters is assigned by processing order.

column1: Explain the different measures of cluster validity. How do you evaluate the clusters generated?
column4:
Why it is hard
  • Clustering is unsupervised, so there is no ground truth to compare against.
  • Any algorithm will return clusters even on random data — so the first question is whether cluster structure exists at all (cluster tendency).
Three families of measure
  • Internal (unsupervised) — uses only the data.
    • Cohesion (compactness): within-cluster SSE. Lower is better.
    • Separation: between-cluster sum of squares. Higher is better.
    • Silhouette coefficient for point \(i\): \[ s = \frac{b-a}{\max(a,b)} \] \(a =\) mean distance to points in its own cluster, \(b =\) mean distance to the nearest other cluster. Range \([-1,1]\); near 1 good, near 0 on a boundary, negative \(=\) probably in the wrong cluster.
  • External (supervised) — compares against known labels.
    • Purity, entropy, precision/recall/F, Rand index, Jaccard coefficient.
  • Relative — compares 2 clusterings, eg by SSE or silhouette, to choose \(K\).
Other issues
  • Determining \(K\) — see the elbow and silhouette methods in §5.2.
  • Scalability: hierarchical is \(O(n^3)\); K-means is linear but needs many passes; BIRCH and CLARA exist to scale.
  • High dimensionality: distances converge \(\rightarrow\) use subspace clustering (CLIQUE) or reduce dimensions first (PCA, Ch 2).
  • Mixed attribute types: needs a mixed dissimilarity measure (Ch 2, §2.4).
  • Outliers distort centroids \(\rightarrow\) K-medoids or DBSCAN.
  • Interpretability: a cluster is only useful if it can be described.

Method
  1. State \(K\) and the initial centroids. Always write down which points you seeded with — the answer depends on it and the examiner needs to follow you.
  2. Build a distance table: every point against every centroid.
  3. Assign each point to its nearest centroid.
  4. Recompute each centroid as the mean of its members.
  5. Repeat until the assignment does not change. That repetition is the convergence proof.
  • You may compare squared distances to avoid square roots — the ordering is identical. Say that you are doing it.

column1: What is anomaly detection? Why is it important?
column4:
Definition
  • An outlier / anomaly is a data object that deviates significantly from the rest, as if generated by a different mechanism.
  • Anomaly detection \(=\) finding those objects.
  • Hawkins: an observation deviating so much that it arouses suspicion it was generated by a different process.
Outlier \(\ne\) noise
  • Noise \(=\) random error / variance in a measured value. Has no meaning, should be removed before mining.
  • Outlier \(=\) a genuine object from a different mechanism. Carries information, and is often the thing you are looking for.
  • Same data point, opposite treatment depending on the task.
  • Related: novelty detection finds genuinely new patterns; once confirmed they are folded into the normal model, so later instances are no longer flagged.
Why it matters / applications
  • Fraud detection: credit-card use unlike the customer's normal pattern.
  • Intrusion detection: traffic unlike normal network behaviour.
  • Medical: unusual symptoms or test results \(\rightarrow\) disease.
  • Public health: a spike in one region \(\rightarrow\) outbreak.
  • Industry: fault and defect detection, equipment failure.
  • Ecosystem disturbance: hurricanes, floods, droughts.
  • Data cleaning: find and remove genuinely erroneous values.
The one-line justification
  • In these applications the rare event is the valuable event. Ordinary mining is tuned to find frequent patterns, so it actively discards exactly what matters here.
Types of outliers (80 Bh asks this directly, 5)
  • Global outlier (point anomaly)
    • Deviates significantly from the rest of the whole data set.
    • Simplest type; most methods target these.
    • Eg a computer broadcasting a huge number of packets in a short time.
  • Contextual (conditional) outlier
    • Deviates significantly with respect to a chosen context.
    • Attributes split into two groups:
      • Contextual attributes: define the context. Eg date, location.
      • Behavioural attributes: what is judged. Eg temperature, humidity.
    • Eg 28\(^\circ\)C is an outlier in a Kathmandu winter, normal in summer.
    • Generalises local outliers; a global outlier is the special case where the context is empty.
Collective: the black group, not any one point. H&K Fig 12.2.
  • Collective outlier
    • A subset of objects that as a whole deviates, even though no individual member is an outlier.
    • Eg 1 delayed shipment is normal; 100 delayed on one day is a collective outlier.
    • Eg a burst of packets from many machines at once \(=\) denial-of-service, though each single packet looks fine.
    • Detecting them needs the relationships between objects (sequence, spatial, graph structure), not just the objects.

    • Training set labelled both normal and outlier \(\rightarrow\) treat as a classification problem.
    • Problem: severe class imbalance (outliers are rare) \(+\) the sample may not represent the outlier distribution.
    • Fixes: oversample outliers, make up artificial outliers, cost-sensitive learning.
  • Semi-supervised
    • Only the normal class is labelled (common in practice).
    • Build a model of normality; anything not matching it is an outlier.
  • Unsupervised
    • No labels at all. Assumes normal objects are far more frequent and cluster together.
    • Most practical, and the default assumption in exam answers.
(B) By the assumption made (this is the “three methods” answer for 78 Bh)
MethodAssumptionWeakness
Statistical (model-based)Normal data follows a stochastic model; low-probability objects are outliers.Must guess the right distribution; poor in high dims.
Proximity-basedAn outlier is far from its neighbours (or in a sparse region).\(O(n^2)\) cost; sensitive to \(r\) and \(k\); struggles w/ varying density (distance-based only).
Clustering-basedNormal objects belong to large, dense clusters; outliers do not.Depends on the clustering; costly; outliers can distort the clusters themselves.
  • Classification-based is sometimes given as a 4th: train a 1-class model of normality (eg 1-class SVM), flag whatever falls outside.

column1: Explain distance-based methods for anomaly detection.
column2: 2+382+61054+3
column4:
Core idea
  • Judge an object by its proximity to its neighbours.
  • An object is an outlier if its neighbourhood is sparse or its neighbours are far.
  • Needs only a distance measure \(\rightarrow\) Ch 2, §2.4, no distribution assumption.
1. Distance-based: the DB\((r,\pi)\) outlier
  • Fix a distance threshold \(r\) (defines the neighbourhood) and a fraction threshold \(\pi\).
  • Object \(o\) is a DB\((r,\pi)\)-outlier if: \[ \frac{\lVert \{o' \mid dist(o,o') \le r\}\rVert}{\lVert D\rVert} \le \pi \]
  • In words: fewer than a \(\pi\) fraction of all objects lie within distance \(r\) of \(o\).
  • Equivalent \(k\)-NN form: with \(k = \lceil \pi\lVert D\rVert \rceil\), object \(o\) is an outlier if \(dist(o, o_k) > r\), where \(o_k\) is its \(k\)th nearest neighbour.
  • Nested-loop algorithm: for each object, scan the others and count how many fall within \(r\); stop early once the count exceeds \(\pi n\). Cost \(O(n^2)\).
2. \(k\)-NN score (the other common phrasing)
  • Score each object by the distance to its \(k\)th nearest neighbour (or the average of its \(k\) nearest).
  • Rank all objects by that score; the top ones are the outliers.
  • 71 Shr asks exactly this, 10.
3. Density-based: the local outlier 80 Bh 3
  • Why needed: distance-based methods take a global view, using one \(r\) for the whole data set.
  • If the data has one dense cluster and one sparse cluster, no single \(r\) works:
    • Set \(r\) small \(\rightarrow\) the entire sparse cluster is wrongly flagged.
    • Set \(r\) large \(\rightarrow\) genuine outliers beside the dense cluster are missed.
  • Fix: compare an object's density to the density of its own neighbours, not to the whole data set.
  • Local Outlier Factor (LOF):
    • \(LOF \approx 1\) \(\rightarrow\) density like its neighbours \(\rightarrow\) normal.
    • \(LOF \gg 1\) \(\rightarrow\) much sparser than its neighbours \(\rightarrow\) outlier.
    • Built from reachability distance and local reachability density.
  • Distance-based finds global outliers; density-based finds local ones. That contrast is the marks.
Strengths / weaknesses
  • \(+\) No distribution assumption; simple; works on any data w/ a distance measure.
  • \(-\) \(O(n^2)\) in the naive form.
  • \(-\) Sensitive to the choice of \(r\), \(\pi\), \(k\).
  • \(-\) Degrades in high dimensions (curse of dimensionality).
Clustering-based 76 Ash short note
  • Cluster the data, then flag as outliers the objects that:
    • belong to no cluster (eg DBSCAN noise points),
    • are far from their own cluster centroid, or
    • belong to a cluster that is very small or very sparse.
  • DBSCAN gives it free: noise points are exactly the outliers. \(\rightarrow\) Ch 5
  • \(+\) Unsupervised; reuses clustering you may already have.
  • \(-\) Effectiveness depends entirely on the clustering; outliers can themselves distort the clusters.
Global vs local, drawn (point 3 above)
\(o_3\), \(o_4\) are far from everything: global outliers, found by DB\((r,\pi)\). \(o_1\), \(o_2\) sit only as far from dense \(C_1\) as ordinary points in sparse \(C_2\) are from each other, so one \(r\) cannot catch them: local outliers, found by LOF. H&K Fig 12.8.
Statistical approaches
  • Assume a model, flag low-probability objects.
  • Parametric: assume a distribution (usually Gaussian), estimate its parameters, flag points in the tails.
    • Common rule: more than 3 standard deviations from the mean.
    • Grubbs' test: detects one outlier at a time in univariate normal data, removes it, repeats. \(H_0\): no outlier.
  • Non-parametric: no assumed shape; use histograms or kernel density estimates.
  • Convex hull method 70 Ch asks this by name verified/added
    • Points on the convex hull (the boundary of the smallest convex polygon enclosing all points) are assumed to be extreme, hence outliers.
    • Peel the hull layer by layer to get successive outlier candidates.
    • Limitation: only ever finds boundary points. An outlier sitting inside the data cloud, in a sparse pocket, is never detected.

    • Common rule: more than 3 standard deviations from the mean.

  • Convex hull method 70 Ch asks this by name verified/added

    • Peel the hull layer by layer to get successive outlier candidates.
    • Limitation: only ever finds boundary points. An outlier sitting inside the data cloud, in a sparse pocket, is never detected.

The model
  • Treat the data set \(D\) as a mixture of two distributions:
    • \(M\) \(=\) the majority (normal) distribution, something tight such as a Gaussian.
    • \(A\) \(=\) the anomaly distribution, taken as uniform because nothing is assumed about how outliers are spread.
  • \(\lambda\) \(=\) prior probability that an object is an anomaly, a small number fixed in advance. \[ D = (1-\lambda)\,M + \lambda\,A \]
  • At any moment the objects are partitioned into \(M_t\) and \(A_t\). Start with \(M_0 = D\) and \(A_0 = \emptyset\): assume everything is normal.
Log-likelihood of the whole data set
\[ LL_t(D) = |M_t|\log(1-\lambda) + \sum_{x_i \in M_t}\log P_{M_t}(x_i) \] \[ \qquad {} + |A_t|\log \lambda + \sum_{x_i \in A_t}\log P_{A_t}(x_i) \]
  • First two terms are the normal account, last two the anomaly account.
Algorithm
  1. \(M \leftarrow D\), \(A \leftarrow \emptyset\), compute \(LL_t(D)\).
  2. For each point \(x \in M\):
    1. Tentatively move \(x\) to \(A\).
    2. Re-estimate \(M\)'s parameters without \(x\) and compute the new \(LL_{t+1}(D)\).
    3. \(\Delta = LL_{t+1}(D) - LL_t(D)\).
    4. If \(\Delta > c\) (a threshold), keep \(x\) in \(A\) and declare it an anomaly; otherwise put it back in \(M\).
  3. Repeat until no point moves.
Why the test works (this is the explanation the marks are for)
  • Moving a normal point out forces \(M\) to explain fewer points it already explained well, and the uniform \(A\) explains it badly \(\rightarrow\) likelihood falls.
  • Moving a genuine outlier out lets \(M\) tighten around the rest, and the outlier was costing \(M\) a huge penalty anyway \(\rightarrow\) likelihood rises sharply.
  • So a large gain in likelihood is itself the evidence that the point does not belong.
Strengths and weaknesses
  • \(+\) Firm statistical footing; gives a principled test rather than an arbitrary distance.
  • \(+\) Handles mixed / categorical attributes if a model exists for them.
  • \(-\) Needs a distribution assumption for \(M\), and a wrong one gives wrong outliers.
  • \(-\) Expensive: \(M\) is re-estimated once per candidate point.
  • \(-\) The threshold \(c\) and the prior \(\lambda\) are both guesses.
  • \(-\) Degrades badly in high dimensions, like every parametric method.

column4:
The fallacy
  • Base rate \(=\) the prior probability of the rare event, eg \(P(\text{intrusion})\).
  • Base rate fallacy \(=\) the tendency to ignore the base rate and judge only by the test's accuracy.
  • Consequence: when the event is very rare, even a highly accurate detector produces mostly false alarms, because the huge normal population generates more false positives than the tiny anomalous population generates true positives.
Set-up (intrusion detection)
  • \(I\) \(=\) intrusive behaviour, \(\lnot I\) \(=\) normal.  \(A\) \(=\) alarm, \(\lnot A\) \(=\) no alarm.
  • Detection rate \(= P(A|I)\)  (true positive rate)
  • False alarm rate \(= P(A|\lnot I)\)
  • Bayesian detection rate \(= P(I|A)\) \(\rightarrow\) what actually matters to the analyst: given an alarm, is it real?
Bayes
\[ P(I|A) = \frac{P(A|I)\,P(I)}{P(A|I)P(I) + P(A|\lnot I)P(\lnot I)} \]
Worked illustration
  • Test 99% accurate both ways, disease prevalence 1 in 100.
  • Then \(P(\text{disease}\mid\text{positive})\) is only about 1/2, not 99%.
  • With a rarer event the result gets far worse.
Axelsson's conclusion
  • In intrusion detection \(P(I)\) is tiny, so the false alarm rate dominates the equation.
  • \(\rightarrow\) you need an extremely low false alarm rate to get a usable Bayesian detection rate. Raw accuracy is not enough.
  • This is the formal reason accuracy is the wrong metric for anomaly detection \(\rightarrow\) same argument as class imbalance in Ch 3, §3.7.

column4:
This chapter is almost entirely theory. Across all 23 papers there is exactly one numerical 76 Ch, on the base rate fallacy. It is solved below, plus 2 practice problems covering the patterns a future numerical would most likely take.
Methods
  • M1 Base rate fallacy: detection rate, false alarm rate, Bayesian detection rate 76 Ch
  • M2 Distance-based outlier: the DB\((r,\pi)\) test practice

Method
  • Let \(I\) \(=\) anomalous, \(\lnot I\) \(=\) normal, \(A\) \(=\) alarm raised.
  • Detection rate \(= P(A|I)\)   False alarm rate \(= P(A|\lnot I)\)
  • Bayesian detection rate (what an analyst actually cares about): \[ P(I|A) = \frac{P(A|I)\,P(I)}{P(A|I)P(I) + P(A|\lnot I)P(\lnot I)} \]
  • Fastest safe route: invent a round population (10,000), build the confusion matrix, read every rate off it. No formula to misremember.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Chaitra · Q11 (b) · [3]
If the probability that a normal object is classified as an anomaly is 0.01 and the probability that an anomalous object is classified as anomalous is 0.99, then what is the false alarm rate and detection rate if 99% of the objects are normal?
column4:
Given
  • \(P(A|\lnot I) = 0.01\)  (normal object raises an alarm)
  • \(P(A|I) = 0.99\)  (anomalous object raises an alarm)
  • \(P(\lnot I) = 0.99\), so \(P(I) = 0.01\)
Step 1: the two rates asked for, read straight off the givens
  • False alarm rate \(= P(A|\lnot I) = \mathbf{0.01}\) (1%)
  • Detection rate \(= P(A|I) = \mathbf{0.99}\) (99%)
Step 2: why the 99% prior was given — build the matrix on 10,000 objects
AlarmNo alarmTotal
Anomalous (\(I\))\(0.99\times100=\mathbf{99}\) (TP)1 (FN)100
Normal (\(\lnot I\))\(0.01\times9900=\mathbf{99}\) (FP)9801 (TN)9,900
Total1989,80210,000
  • Check: detection rate \(=99/100=0.99\) ✓  false alarm rate \(=99/9900=0.01\) ✓
Step 3: Bayesian detection rate
\[ P(I|A) = \frac{(0.99)(0.01)}{(0.99)(0.01) + (0.01)(0.99)} = \frac{0.0099}{0.0099+0.0099} = \frac{99}{198} = \mathbf{0.50} \]
Final answer
  • False alarm rate \(= \mathbf{0.01}\), detection rate \(= \mathbf{0.99}\).
  • But the Bayesian detection rate is only 0.50 — half of every alarm raised is false, despite a detector that is 99% accurate in both directions.
  • This is the base rate fallacy. The normal population (9,900) is so much larger than the anomalous one (100) that its 1% error rate manufactures exactly as many false alarms (99) as there are true detections (99).
  • Say this in the exam: it is the whole point of the question and is worth more than the two arithmetic lines.
If the examiner wanted only the two conditional rates, they are given directly and the question is trivial — which is the clue that the 99% prior must be used for something. Answer both readings: state the two rates, then compute \(P(I|A)\) and name the fallacy. verified/added

Shows how fast the Bayesian rate collapses. verified/added
  • On 100,000 objects: 100 anomalous, 99,900 normal.
  • TP \(=0.99\times100 = 99\)   FP \(=0.01\times99{,}900 = 999\)
  • \(P(I|A) = \dfrac{99}{99+999} = \dfrac{99}{1098} = \mathbf{0.090}\)

  • Conclusion (Axelsson): to keep \(P(I|A)\) usable when \(P(I)\) is tiny you must drive the false alarm rate down, not push the detection rate up.

column4:
Method

column1: What is Web Mining? Briefly explain the structure / taxonomy of Web Mining.
column4:
Definition
  • Web mining \(=\) applying data mining to discover patterns from web data: the content, the link structure and the usage logs.
Why the Web is hard (good opening lines)
  • Huge, growing, and widely distributed.
  • Semi-structured / unstructured (HTML, not tables).
  • Highly dynamic; heterogeneous; multilingual.
  • Only a tiny fraction is relevant to any one user.
  • Broad topics return hundreds of thousands of documents \(\rightarrow\) search returns too much, and misses too much.
The taxonomy, drawn
The three branches and their sub-branches, exactly the list on the right. Draw this tree first, then explain each box. Mishra's Ch 6 & 7 notes, p6.
The taxonomy (3 branches — this IS the answer)
  1. Web Content Mining: mine the content of pages (text, images, video).
    • Web page content mining: extract facts from within pages.
    • Search result mining: summarise / cluster / categorise results.
  2. Web Structure Mining: mine the hyperlink graph.
    • Links carry authority: a link is a vote.
    • Algorithms: PageRank, HITS, CLEVER.
    • Finds authoritative pages, hubs, and web communities.
  3. Web Usage Mining: mine the server logs / click-streams.
    • General access pattern tracking: how the site is used overall.
    • Customised usage tracking: per-user personalisation.
    • Uses: site restructuring, recommendation, targeted ads, caching, fraud detection.
PageRank (asked as a short note in 2 papers + 1 numerical)
  • Ranks a page by who links to it, not by what it says.
  • Two ideas:
    1. A link from page \(T\) to page \(A\) is a vote for \(A\).
    2. Votes are weighted by the voter's own rank, and split across all its outgoing links.
  • Recursive: a page is important if important pages point to it.
\[ PR(A) = (1-d) + d\sum_{i}\frac{PR(T_i)}{C(T_i)} \]
  • \(T_i\) \(=\) pages linking to \(A\); \(C(T_i)\) \(=\) number of outbound links from \(T_i\).
  • \(d\) \(=\) damping factor, usually 0.85.
  • Random surfer model: with probability \(d\) the surfer follows a link, with probability \((1-d)\) they jump to a random page.
  • Why damping is needed: without it, a group of pages linking only to each other would hoard all the rank (a “rank sink”), and pages with no outlinks would leak it.
  • Computed iteratively until the values settle; ranks converge quickly.
HITS (for contrast)
  • Two scores per page: authority (pointed to by good hubs) and hub (points to good authorities).
  • Query-dependent and computed at query time; PageRank is query-independent and precomputed.
Text mining 81 Ba 4
  • Key steps:
    1. Text preprocessing: tokenise, remove stop words, stemming (reduce to root form), case folding.
    2. Feature/attribute generation: build the term vector (bag of words).
    3. Feature selection: drop uninformative terms; weight by TF–IDF.
    4. Mining: classification, clustering, association, topic modelling.
    5. Analysis / interpretation of the results.
  • Similarity between documents \(\rightarrow\) cosine similarity \(\rightarrow\) Ch 2, §2.4.
  • Information retrieval measures: precision and recall \(\rightarrow\) Ch 3, §3.7.
Mining object and multimedia data 634
PIN 3 75 Ash, 74 Ch, 75 Ch
  • Multimedia data \(=\) image, audio, video, text-plus-media in digital form.
  • Feature extraction first — you never mine the raw pixels:
    • Image: colour histogram, texture, shape, edges.
    • Audio: pitch, frequency, MFCC.  Video: motion vectors, key frames.
  • Tasks: similarity search (content-based retrieval), classification, clustering, association among media features, video-shot detection.
  • Challenges: very high dimensionality, huge volume, and the semantic gap — low-level features do not map cleanly to human meaning.
Visual data mining 75 Ch short note 4
  • Uses visualisation to help the user discover knowledge, combining human perception with machine computation.
  • Categories: data visualisation, mining-result visualisation, mining-process visualisation, and interactive visual mining.
  • Techniques: scatter plots, box plots, parallel coordinates, pixel-oriented, dendrograms.
  • Why it works: humans spot patterns and outliers in a picture far faster than in a table.

column1: Explain time series data mining with an example.
column4:
Definition
  • A time series is a sequence of values recorded at successive, usually equal, time intervals.
  • Time-series data mining \(=\) finding patterns, trends and regularities in such data.
  • Eg stock prices, daily temperature, sales per month, sensor readings, ECG, network traffic, power consumption.
  • What makes it different: the order matters and consecutive values are correlated, so the usual “independent tuples” assumption breaks.
The 4 components of a time series (memorise: T-C-S-I)
  • Trend (T): the long-term overall direction. Eg steady sales growth.
  • Cyclic (C): long, irregular swings, over years. Eg business cycles.
  • Seasonal (S): regular, calendar-fixed variation. Eg umbrella sales in monsoon.
  • Irregular / random (I): residual noise left after the other three.
  • Models: multiplicative \(Y = T \times C \times S \times I\), or additive \(Y = T+C+S+I\).
A stock price series (solid) and its 10-day moving average (dashed): smoothing strips the irregular part and leaves the trend. H&K Fig 13.2.
Tasks
  • Trend analysis \(+\) forecasting (moving average, exponential smoothing, ARIMA).
  • Similarity search: find series that behave alike.
    • Whole-sequence matching vs subsequence matching.
    • Needs normalisation (offset and amplitude) first, else scale dominates.
    • Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) aligns series that are out of phase or run at different speeds — Euclidean distance cannot. verified/added
  • Motif discovery: repeated subsequences.   Anomaly detection: unusual subsequences \(\rightarrow\) Ch 6.
  • Segmentation and classification of series.
Smoothing: moving average
  • Replace each value by the mean of a window around it \(\rightarrow\) removes the irregular component and exposes the trend.
  • A larger window smooths more but lags more.
Example to quote
  • Daily closing prices of a share over 5 years: the trend is the multi-year rise, the seasonal part is the recurring festival-quarter bump, the cyclic part is the multi-year market swing, and a one-day crash is irregular. Mining finds the trend for forecasting and the crash as an anomaly.

column1: Chapter 7 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4: This chapter is almost entirely short notes. Across all 23 papers there is exactly one numerical 76 Ch, on PageRank. It is solved in full below, plus 1 practice problem on the variant most likely to be set next.

Method
\[ PR(A) = (1-d) + d\sum_{i}\frac{PR(T_i)}{C(T_i)} \]
  1. Write down the link table first: for every page, its outlinks (to get \(C\)) and its inlinks (to know which terms to sum). Nearly every error comes from confusing the two.
  2. Initialise all ranks (here 0.25).
  3. Each iteration, compute all pages using the previous iteration's values, then substitute in together.
  4. Repeat for the required number of iterations, or until the values settle.
  • A page's own rank is split equally among its outlinks — that is the \(/C(T_i)\).
  • A page with no inlinks sits permanently at \((1-d) = 0.15\).

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Chaitra · Q12 · [8]
Consider the following subset of pages and their links. Apply the PageRank algorithm using a damping factor of 0.85. A minimum of five iterations are required. Assume initial page rank of all pages is 0.25.
column4:
Step 1: read the graph

BC1A
CA1A, B, D
DC1none
Step 2: write the 4 equations
(\(d = 0.85\), \(1-d = 0.15\))
  • \(PR(A) = 0.15 + 0.85\,PR(C)\)
  • \(PR(B) = 0.15 + 0.85\,\dfrac{PR(A)}{2}\)
  • \(PR(C) = 0.15 + 0.85\Big(\dfrac{PR(A)}{2} + PR(B) + PR(D)\Big)\)
  • \(PR(D) = 0.15 + 0.85(0) = \mathbf{0.15}\) constant, D has no inlinks
  • Note \(A\)'s rank is divided by 2 because A links to both B and C.
Step 3: iterate

10.36250.25630.68130.1500

Row 0 is the given start value.
Sample working (iteration 1)
  • \(PR(A) = 0.15 + 0.85(0.25) = 0.3625\)
  • \(PR(B) = 0.15 + 0.85(0.25/2) = 0.2563\)
  • \(PR(C) = 0.15 + 0.85(0.125+0.25+0.25) = 0.6813\)
  • \(PR(D) = 0.15\)
Final answer after 5 iterations
  • \(PR(A)=0.972\), \(PR(B)=0.519\), \(PR(C)=1.028\), \(PR(D)=0.150\)
  • Ranking: C \(>\) A \(>\) B \(>\) D
Two comments worth writing, they show understanding. verified/added
1. The values are still climbing at iteration 5 but the ranking has been stable since iteration 3. PageRank converges on order much faster than on value, which is why 5 iterations is enough for the question.
2. Solving the equations exactly gives the fixed point \(PR(A)=1.490\), \(PR(B)=0.783\), \(PR(C)=1.577\), \(PR(D)=0.150\), and these sum to \(\mathbf{4.00} = N\). That sum is your check — in this (non-normalised) form the ranks always converge to the number of pages.
3. C wins because it collects links from three pages while A collects only one, and D is stuck at 0.15 because nothing points to it. Linking out never raises your own rank.

Repeat Problem 1.1 on the same four-page graph, but using the normalised PageRank formula \[ PR(A) = \frac{1-d}{N} + d\sum_i \frac{PR(T_i)}{C(T_i)} \] with \(d = 0.85\), \(N = 4\) and an initial rank of 0.25 for every page. Compare the converged ranks and the ordering with those of Problem 1.1.
column4:
This form makes the ranks sum to 1 instead of \(N\). Know both. verified/added
  • With \(N=4\), \(\frac{1-d}{N} = \frac{0.15}{4} = 0.0375\).
  • Iteration 1 from the same 0.25 start:
    • \(PR(A) = 0.0375 + 0.85(0.25) = 0.2500\)
    • \(PR(B) = 0.0375 + 0.85(0.125) = 0.1438\)
    • \(PR(C) = 0.0375 + 0.85(0.625) = 0.5688\)
    • \(PR(D) = 0.0375\)
  • Sum \(= 1.0001 \approx 1\) ✓ — that is the check for this form.
  • The ranking is identical (C \(>\) A \(>\) B \(>\) D); only the scale differs.
  • In the exam: state which form you are using in one line. Either is accepted; mixing them is not.
